utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, continue with your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, to continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not having any English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was the wrong channel, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was receiving it on the B/C/S channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On Friday we left off with your visits to Kosovo in early 1999 when you and other deputy Prime Ministers spoke and toured several towns of the province at the time, and I quoted to you, among other things, several sentences from what your colleague Professor Ratko Markovic said, and that was contained in tab 2. Tab 2 contains a special edition that covered your visit to Kosovo and Metohija at the time. The point of what I intend to ask you is in the passage that I'm going to quote now. It's on page 606. That's where we left off last time. Your colleague Professor Ratko Markovic says: "Kosovo and Metohija is an ethnically heterogeneous area and has to stay that way. Anyone who tries to ethnically cleanse this area will fail." And he added that: "History made this area ethnically diverse and the structure cannot be changed. The Albanians are those that have to prove that they wish peaceful co-existence with other ethnic communities." Tell me, in your public and political work, when did you first come across this idea of ethnically pure Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a fairly old idea. It dates back to the time of Tito's communist regime. After World War II, the communist regime banned the return of all Serbs who had been expelled from Kosovo and Metohija during the war, and there were more than 100.000 of them. At the time, Italian occupants and quisling forces, so-called Ballisti, made up of Albanian fascists, expelled Serbs and seized their property in order to change the ethnic structure of Kosovo in an accelerated way for the purpose of negotiations after the war, especially in the case of defeat by their allies. That's an option they had in mind. Before the war, the ethnic structure of Kosovo was even. There was an equal proportion of Serbs, Gorani, Romas and others. They made up about half, and the other half were Albanians. This structure was upset after the war. The communists made this worse by banning the return of the Serbs by law. Their property was never returned. After that, communists invented a special autonomous area called Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija. That was a lower degree than Vojvodina had, all the way until the constitution of 1963. Under the 1963 constitution, the autonomous status of Kosovo and Metohija was made equal to that of Vojvodina. The then regime under Tito gave absolute power to Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija, and they started exerting pressure on Serbs and other ethnic communities to leave Kosovo, whereas a large number of Albanian immigrants were coming from Albania. Many of them were running away from the communist dictatorship of Enver Hoxha, which was much harder to bear than Tito's regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this objective of ethnically pure Kosovo, various public figures wrote about it in the 1980s. Do you remember at the time in the SFRY there was a very renowned theoretical magazine called Socialism?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in that magazine and in the broader public the objective of Albanian separatists to create an ethnically pure Kosovo was well known?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 1989, it was a forbidden subject that nobody dared to write about in books, magazines, or newspapers. The regime punished anyone who tried to write about it. We have a famous case of Dobrica Cosic who raised the issue in 1968. He was then member of the Central Committee of the Communist Party. He was immediately replaced, placed under surveillance by the police, and harassed in all sorts of ways. The regime tried to show on the example of Dobrica Cosic what would happen to anyone if they only try to raise the issue of Albanian separatism in Kosovo and Metohija. Later on, the communist regime showed its intention in 1971 to grant Kosovo the status of a state. Some professors at the law faculty led by Professor Djuric, Kosta Cavoski, and many others, opposed the draft constitutional amendments publicly. Professor Djuric was expelled from the law faculty, as well as his colleagues, and until the change in government, they were unable to return to their posts. So the regime punished anyone who tried to speak publicly about the problems in Kosovo and Metohija all the way until 1981 when the famous, notorious demonstrations happened in Kosovo. It was only then that the Yugoslav public started to discuss the problem more publicly. And then all sorts of facts started to emerge. We began to hear about the personal experience of many expelled and persecuted Serbs, even persecuted Albanians. There was Professor Halit Trnavci, a renowned professor who had to flee from Kosovo and Metohija because he propounded the idea that the future of Kosovo Albanians was to have a peaceful co-existence with the Serbs because their life in Kosovo was better than in Albania under Enver Hoxha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your colleague, professor of constitutional law from Slovenia, Ivan Kristan, testified here before you. In 1981 -- and I have in front of me the magazine called Socialism that I just mentioned, issue number 10 from 1981. In 1981 when, as you said very correctly, the discussion began in Yugoslavia about this clearly expressed intention to have an ethnically pure Kosovo, and I will quote from his article in the magazine Socialism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... quoted, the appropriate course is for them to be made available to the Prosecution at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Milosevic well knows that. Do you have copies available, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. I do, if you're interested, several copies. It's the magazine Socialism from 1981, issue number 10. I just have the article written by one of your witnesses, Ivan Kristan, who wrote about this in 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will quote to you, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would appreciate to have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are to wait until we have received the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it's in the Serbian language, so you will not be able to read it, but we can put this passage on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, please find page 1733.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Albanian nationalist idea about the ethnically pure Kosovo and the unification --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. We cannot do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you're being asked by the interpreters to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have slowed down a little. "The slogan about ethnically pure Kosovo offers, instead of real equality of nations and nationalities, constant counting and chauvinism."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, Was it clear already in the early 1980s that there was very public discussion about this very public objective of ethnically pure Kosovo that was held by Albanian separatists?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in 1981, between Serbian, Croatian, Muslim, Slovene, Macedonian, and all other politicians, there was absolutely no difference in the assessment of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. At least in their declarations they were against Albanian separatism, against non-observance of civil rights and freedoms, and it seemed in that 1981 all Yugoslav units will help to fight this Albanian separatism in its purist form, and it had already begun to express itself in street violence. Another thing was clear: All Albanian separatists in 1981 come on as Marxist-Leninist revolutionaries drawing their ideas from Enver Hoxha. Even then, under the communist regime, that was untenable because the regime itself had begun to give way under the pressure of the struggle for basic rights and freedoms. In the territory of the former Yugoslavia, consensus had already been reached that there was no return to -- to Stalinism, and the orientation was towards liberalisation. I personally think under mono-party system that was impossible, but anyway, that was the thrust of the thinking then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at another two passages that I wish to draw your attention to, and you will see that Ivan Kristan gives us certain numbers as indicators of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kristan says if Albanians in Kosovo are not equal because they do not have a republic, the question has to be asked how would they then fare with other nations and communities in that republic? When I say nationalities, I mean ethnic minorities. That was socialist lingo for minority. The answer is that other minorities would also have to get a state, because the same criterion has to apply to everyone, not only to Kosovo. And then we would have several autonomous republics. He says ethnic head counts are especially fatal to such units as these provinces. There is a lot of pressure and chauvinist incidents that even lead some communities to leave because they cannot suffer it any longer. That already happened in Kosovo out of where thousands of Serbs and Montenegrins have already left. So that compared to 1971, in 1981 Serbs and Montenegrins are much fewer. And he gives specific data: In 1971, Serbs were 18.3 per cent; Montenegrins 2.5 per cent; whereas in 1981 these figures were 13.2 and 1.7. And even in absolute terms, the percentage of Serbs and Montenegrins were much fewer; 8.1 per cent and 4.8 per cent, whereas the number of Albanians rose by 34 per cent. At the time, Mr. Kristan behaves as a well-informed scholar and provides real facts. However, later he changed his position by 180 per cent [as interpreted]. He starts supporting Albanian nationalism and goes against everything he said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to those terms "ethnically pure" and "ethnic cleansing." Was there anyone in Yugoslavia at the time who did not condemn such backward approach to the resolution of national problems?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said this. Politicians from Macedonia, Slovenia, Muslim politicians, Serbs, Croatians, everybody came out in force against ethnically pure Kosovo and the objective of ethnic cleansing that was held by Albanian separatists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you given this any thought? How come ten years later it was precisely the Serbs, who had faced that evil and fought against that evil, in whose public opinion ethnic cleansing was considered to be a dirty kind of behaviour, criminal conduct? How come it was the Serbs whose behaviour was found objectionable and who were accused of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because later on the Western powers and the Vatican started interfering in internal Yugoslav affairs with a view to breaking up Yugoslavia, and that is when the Western services started working in terms of conducting a psychological warfare. And they launched the most terrible slogans in order to blacken the name of the Serbs as a people. Because in the West it was thought that it was the Serbs who truly cared about Yugoslavia and who were the only ones who were prepared to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. energetically fight for the survival of Yugoslavia, that all others could be instructed in terms of pursuing the Western policy of breaking up Yugoslavia. So everything that was negative in the past in different parts of Yugoslavia was subsequently ascribed to the Serbs as their intention, as their objective, as their will, as their plan, as their design, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you say there was a deliberate attempt on the part of the West to demonise, blacken the name of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That plan existed first in Vatican, in Germany, and then all other Western powers joined in. Until 1991, America was vacillating, wondering whether to go for the break-up of Yugoslavia or not. It seemed to me at one point in time that America's objective was to -- to have Yugoslavia survive but to have the communist system collapse. However, since Germany and Vatican had the primary role of all political process in the Balkans at the time and since they had prepared their agencies to carry out these plans, America subsequently started pursuing this kind of policy, and they even played a very prominent role in pursuing such a policy later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a general question, Mr. Seselj. If we look at this entire decade from 1990 until 2000 in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, at any point in time, even while the wars were raging in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, during this crisis was there ever any idea, and in particular was any idea materialised in terms of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Chamber is happy to receive and interested in receiving this highly generalised form of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was just about to bring that to the attention of Mr. Milosevic. I have allowed this evidence because I know it's part of your case, but in my judgement, we have had enough of it and you must bring the witness now to evidence that more directly bears on the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the Chamber's ruling. My two observations would have been both that it verges on expert without the advantage of a properly footnoted expert report in advance; alternatively, if it's going to contain sweeping observations of the kind made at all, those observations are valueless unless we know the evidential source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Bring the witness, as I said, to evidence that more directly relates to the indictment. We have had enough general information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, take a look at tab number 1 first. Tell me, what does it contain?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That tab contains a conference or, rather, a broadcast that Dr. Ratko Markovic, Dr. Milovan Bojic, and I -- Zoran Andjelkovic was there too, president of the Provisional Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija. This is a TV programme on TV Pristina that we had on the 15th of January. That was the same day when the government session was held in Pristina. After the government session, since we were staying on in Kosovo and Metohija as the rest of the government members returned to Belgrade, we stayed at the police headquarters for a long time, then took a stroll in the streets of Pristina also for quite awhile, about an hour, hour and a half, and then we finally went to TV Pristina where we had a live television programme, answering the questions of spectators. There's a mistake in this tab. I don't think it exists in the English translation. I think the English translation is complete as far as I managed to see. However, in the original, every second page is missing. I don't know whether I'm the only one who has this mistake here or whether you have the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have the same mistake here in my texts. They probably thought that they could print on both pages. So the Serbian text is rather useless. Tell me, what was the point of your speech in public then as well as of the other participants? You were politically active as deputy Prime Minister, together with other members of the government. What was the main message conveyed by what you were saying then?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke in unison, although we had different ideological orientations. First of all, we wanted the general situation in Kosovo and Metohija to calm down. We want dialogue between the Serbian and Albanian political representatives and the representatives of the other ethnic communities in Kosovo and Metohija. We want all forms of terrorism to be brought to an end. We were persuading Albanians that terrorism was not in their interests, that the interference of Western powers was not in their interest. We were saying that the Western powers are trying to take advantage of the situation and of them for their own purposes and that finally they will be deeply harmed in their national interests, just like the Serbs. At any rate, our mission was a mission of calming the situation down and one of persuasion. We were promising various representatives of the government that we would invest more in Kosovo and Metohija and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We now have the point of tab 1. Move to the next tab, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Seselj, the members of the government of Serbia, did they have a press conference on the 17th of January at the end of their visit?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a press conference at the Pristina media centre. We presented our view of the overall situation, our experience after our visit to Kosovo and Metohija. We explained to journalists from home and abroad what the point of our visit was. We presented our view that we would come again, that we would have government sessions held in different towns in Kosovo and Metohija. However, at that press conference there was reference to the action in Racak that had just happened. We explained what had happened in Racak. We already had information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in tab 31 is there a transcript of the press conference that was published in the newspaper Velika Srbija under the headlines "The CIA is Operating Through William Walker"?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the complete transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the press conference was held on the 17th of January.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Two days after the events in Racak. What did you conclude then?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We concluded that our police had set out in action to break up a terrorist gang that had previously killed one or two policemen, I cannot remember exactly now. Previously, our police had informed the OSCE Verification Mission that they were setting out on this action. The OSCE verifiers were present while this action was being carried out. Of course they were not on the actual site where they could get killed, because they were always trying to spare themselves, but they were close enough to see that there was fierce fighting and that shooting was coming from both sides. In this action, our police sustained small losses, and they managed to overcome the Albanian terrorist gang. The Albanian terrorists had greater -- a greater number of casualties. It kept changing from 40 to 50, all the way up to 80 and so on. At any rate, it was a resounding defeat of the Albanian terrorists. Only terrorists got killed. Not a single civilian was killed. Of course, there were terrorists who fought in civilian clothing. When the fighting was over sometime in the evening, our police collected the weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't see how Mr. Seselj's evidence about Racak is going to help your case. You have other witnesses who can testify and who have testified more directly to the events in Racak. The provision of mere general information is not going to advance your case. His views on Racak I don't find very -- very helpful. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is, however, one specific question I would like to ask you about Racak, very specific. You said that by the time of the press conference you had certain information. Now, what was the time of day at which the press conference took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could have been around midday. I don't know exactly. I cannot remember exactly now. Noon, 1.00 p.m., around that time day. Around midday. I don't know the exact hour. But this is the 17th, whereas the action in Racak took place on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My specific question is what was the source of your information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our police. General Vlastimir Djordjevic, General Sreten Lukic. During my previous testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you speak to each of these gentlemen prior to the 17th of January on the subject of Racak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can give you the details, which will be very telling evidence about this. I've already said that on the 16th of January, a day after the action in Racak, General Vlastimir Djordjevic, Vojislav Zivkovic, Sonija Stjepanovic, and I travelled on a police helicopter from Pristina to Prizren. When we came to Pristina again, General Vlastimir Djordjevic told me that as a matter of fact on the following day, after returning from Prizren to Pristina by helicopter, he flew over Racak, that he saw a lot foreign journalists there, verifiers, et cetera. That's one more detail. I've already told you that during lunch at police headquarters in Pristina we received our initial information about fighting with terrorists in Racak. But Mr. Milosevic's question has to do with what I stated at the press conference. You will see this on page 50 in the original. I don't know where it is in the English translation, but it's towards the end. I talk about the action in Racak there as something that is called trigger event, a trigger event in US military terminology. You understand it probably better than I do because my knowledge of English is not that good. You know that the CIA organised massacres in the market of Markale in Sarajevo, in Vasa Miskin Street, at the Partizan cemetery. That's what I say here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please remember the question that was asked. You say that you mention this towards the end of your press conference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you use the word "trigger." Can you show me where that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I didn't use the word at the press conference but I'm explaining the phenomenon to you so that it would be clear to you. I'm trying to explain to you the deception with the Markale market in Sarajevo because already by then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I've got a very specific matter I want to deal with and I would be grateful if you would concentrate on it. I simply wanted to know the source of your information. You've answered it, and we can now move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, in relation to your objection as to why I'm asking Seselj about Racak, you should bear in mind that, since he was deputy Prime Minister at the time, he received all information that was topical in the area. What he knew was what the government knew. And what he knew and what the government of Serbia knew had to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, very well, put your questions and let us hear the evidence which he has on Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you had all information about Racak. In view of regular practice, in view of your position, in view of government behaviour, in view of the overall situation, could it have happened at all that you would not receive accurate information about this but that you'd receive wrong information?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this would have been absolutely impossible. I am a person who is so well-informed that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer that. Could it have happened that you would not have received wrong information? That really is not a useful question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this event in Racak was taken advantage of in order to try to ascribe a crime to our state, a crime that had not been committed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even while we were in Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's again a leading -- ridiculous leading question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, this practice and this event in Racak, was this a solitary example of a special interpretation of events in the territory of the former Yugoslavia? I'm not describing it at all now.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even while our -- us three deputy Prime Ministers were there in Kosovo, the Verification Mission and William Walker spoke up, saying that this was a massacre. We had information that this was fighting. The Verification Mission knew about that fighting. Despite the facts, they immediately started accusing the Serbs of a massacre. That is why at the press conference I said that this was not the first time that this happened to us; that similar things happened at the Markale market in Sarajevo, at the Vasa Miskin Street in Sarajevo, and so on, that various events were staged in order to condemn the Serb side in all these situations of war or in all these incidents. Then I say that the situation was similar with the CIA agents and proteges in Iraq and that it had been exposed in the UN at that time. Then I talk about Walker's behaviour in Kosovo and Metohija in general. And you know what the role of this Walker was in Latin America. You know all the dirty things he took part in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Obviously insofar as the accused and the witness regard it as in his or either of their interests to advance these generalities and the Court doesn't wish to stop them, that's their choice, but really, this can't help us in our inquiry into the events to hear these general views of this man about the CIA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Milosevic. We have had enough of this general information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could give you some very concrete information, Mr. Robinson, if you wish, and it has to do with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in response to questions from Mr. Milosevic or from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you mentioned a particular expression of staging events, when you were giving various examples. As deputy Prime Minister of the government of Serbia, did you know anything about some kind of transport of corpses from Kosovo to other parts of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no transport of corpses that would involve the government or any other government body. I can guarantee that. Corpses were transported by those who wanted them to be found at a certain moment, who wanted to find them in the place where they buried them in order to use this for their own political ends. As the deputy Prime Minister, a document came into my hands dated the 12th of August, 1998. The Republican Committee in the US Congress submitted a report to Congress saying that in Kosovo and Metohija this trigger event was needed, something like what the Muslims had done in Sarajevo, in order for public opinion to turn against the Serbs. This is mentioned in the report submitted to Congress on the 12th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I regret having to intervene more than is my wont, but first of all, the question was interestingly leading by asking about staging an event and then asking about something else, but passing on from that, if the witness is going to raise as a proposition that the transportation of bodies was other than by those acting on the accused's behalf, I'm sure we'd all be very interested in knowing what the hard evidence for that proposition is. But it doesn't seem to me that the trigger event referred to in the document of the 12th of August, 1998, is going to get us much further. What we'd all like to hear is what the hard evidence is that other parties unknown, who have been rather obliquely referred to thus far, actually moved these bodies. Very interested in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's a matter that you could raise in cross-examination, but I'll ask it now from the Bench. Mr. Seselj, what is the source for your claim that there were other persons or other bodies that were responsible for the transportation of bodies and that they had particular purposes in mind? What is the evidential basis for that? This is an important part of the case, and if you have evidence on that, then give it us to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have evidence. As deputy Prime Minister of Serbia, I received information that the CIA had formed a special operations group, the aim of which was to topple Slobodan Milosevic and his party. This group was headed by John Deutsche, the seat of the group was in Vienna. As deputy Prime Minister of Serbia, I learned that leaders of the pro-Western opposition political parties were going there to receive instructions. As deputy Prime Minister of Serbia, I learned from our own intelligence agencies that the CIA had recruited Jovica Stanisic and Momcilo Perisic. They were the chief of intelligence and the Chief of the General Staff respectively, and they joined in this activity in toppling Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have not yet given us information about the transportation of bodies. Are you coming to that? This is what I asked you about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm giving you this information now. I'm telling you now, and I'll come to it, certainly I will, Mr. Robinson. I will tell you everything I know. I'll be very happy to tell you. If I speak too broadly, I do apologise. It may be a professional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you are speaking too broadly. Just give us the information you have about the transportation of bodies by other persons and the specific ends that they had in mind. Forget the introduction. We don't want the introduction, just give us the hard evidence if there is any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let Mr. Seselj answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, my answer can be correct only if it's complete. So I ask you to bear with me for a minute and I will give you a complete response to this question, which is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have background. The background, as you say, is a conspiracy by the USA to subvert Mr. Milosevic. You also mentioned certain persons in Yugoslavia who were being instructed by the CIA. We have -- we have the background, now give us the evidence about the transportation of bodies by other persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 5th of October, during the pro-Western Mafia putsch, several generals of the police reveal themselves to be on the side of those perpetrating the putsch. They were given positions in the new pro-Western regime. No one held them responsible, but had there been any transportation of bodies, they would have had to have direct responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. That's your own interpretation and assessment of the event. You have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have more evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not evidence. That's just an opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, another piece of evidence is that no one in Serbia has been tried for transporting bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do have specific evidence, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a corpse belonging to Dibran Dani. He was buried by our authorities on 5th of June, 1999. And there is complete documentation about how he came to be killed. His photograph was taken. All information was taken, samples and so on, everything was done according to the law. And he was buried near Izbica in Kosovo and Metohija. Later on he was found in Petrovo Selo in Serbia, near the Danube. Why would it be in the interest of our government that a corpse that was buried once along with documentation, photographs, and so on - and there are photographs, you can get them from the police in Belgrade - why would this body be disinterred and transferred to Petrovo Selo near the Danube? There's no logic in it. This man's name is Dibran Dani. He was exhumed in Izbica. The cemetery where was he found was photographed. There was a visual inspection of the body. A post-mortem was carried out, and he was then buried in the Muslim cemetery in the village of Nevoljane. There is a photograph of his grave. There are official records and photographs of all this. This body was buried on the 5th of June, 1999, just before the arrival of KFOR, the occupiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I take it, then, that your answer is merely to raise the question as to why would these bodies have been transported. You have raised the question. That is the question which we are investigating, and I had gathered that you had some evidence on it, but you don't appear to. Mr. Milosevic, move on to the next issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in connection with this I will put a few questions to you. What do you know about these refrigerator trucks with corpses and the unearthing of corpses in Batajnica and other places in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The story about the corpses was first launched by a certain Oskar Kliper from Zajecar, and he was working in the state security service, he and his son. They worked in Kosovo and Metohija and they stole some gold. For this reason, they were expelled from the service. This Oskar Kliper changed his name. He took a Serbian name officially and started publishing a magazine dealing with crime, and he launched this story of corpses, and this was something that was very interesting for the Serbian public. If someone wants to hide corpses, and if it's the state who wants to do this, the state has many means at its disposal. We have crematoria in many cemeteries, and in Serbia many deceased are cremated. This can be done at any cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, why would Oskar - I don't have the last name - this gentleman, why would he have launched this story about corpses? What was his purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He launched this story in order for the Serb public to be amazed and to justify the kidnapping of Slobodan Milosevic and his transfer to The Hague. After this was done, the story died down. There are no results of the public investigation as to who transported the bodies. The corpses were identified and taken back to Kosovo and Metohija and so on. However, the people who organised the transport of these bodies later remained in the top of the regime. It's impossible that there is no proof of this. Who transported these bodies in a refrigerator truck? Had somebody done this and taken the bodies out, that could be explained, but for someone to push a whole refrigerator truck into the Danube, which has a variable water level, that's beyond any logic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this kind of evidence isn't helping your case at all. It's just speculation. Anybody can come here and offer you their views as to why bodies were transported. If Mr. Seselj doesn't have any evidence on the subject matter, then move on to another area. You can make those points in your closing address, the points that he's making. Make them in your closing address to us. That's the proper place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no intention of burdening myself with this nonsense that Mr. Nice is trying to stage here. Mr. Seselj mentioned Dibran Dani --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... observation to be sanctioned. It's not an appropriate course for an accused like this accused to make the suggestion that I am staging evidence. I am presenting evidence. He knows it and it's up to him to produce evidence that deals with it. Can I make another point which I was going to defer until cross-examination, but I understand from the projected time that this witness is going to take that we are going to be listening to him in chief before I get to cross-examination for another three days or thereabouts. He's speaking at a very high volume. It's not necessary. It actually makes the process of attending to his words very much more difficult, and I would invite the Chamber to invite him to use a more moderate level of voice in order to assist us. It will not do to say he can't do that. He can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Two matters first, Mr. Milosevic. Your comment about the staging of evidence by the Prosecutor was inappropriate. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Secondly, Mr. Seselj, it is true your decibel level is a little high. When Mr. Nice raised that matter the first day you gave evidence, I remarked that in my view it was your natural tone of voice, but it is a little difficult to follow the evidence because you speak so loudly. So I'm going to ask you to speak a little more softly so that we can attend more closely to the interpreters, because your decibel level is colliding with the transmission of the interpretation. So please speak a little more softly. And, Mr. Milosevic, let us move to another area and see whether we can have evidence that is more directly related to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, first of all in connection to Mr. Nice's observation, Mr. Seselj speaks loudly. It's a habit he has. I have never heard him speak softly. Asking him to whisper now I think is completely inappropriate. As you know, "consuetudo quasi altera natura." It's his nature. It's his habit. He's speaking in a natural way for him. He is not speaking especially loudly for your sake. As for the other observation, I'm asking him whether he has any evidence that our state organs did not conceal bodies but that on the contrary, official records were left, photographs and so on and so forth. This contradicts what Mr. Nice has said. Mr. Seselj mentioned the case of this man --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 24, Mr. Seselj, if you would be kind enough to look at it, there is a report about the forensic report of the site, and here you have the case of Dibran Dani in tab 24. You also have a report on the forensic inspection of the site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not translated. If you have a short passage, then you know our procedure. It's to be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This cumulatively shows that the state left traces about people who were killed. There is a report of the on-site investigation. Mr. Seselj, look: First you have the report in this tab. Then you have a form, and then you have a diagram showing the disposition of the graves, and then you have photographs. I assume the diagram and the photographs need not be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I am just being shown the index which indicates that this document was already admitted in the evidence, testimony of Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we recognised this yesterday and Ms. Dicklich invited the accused's associates to make the document available to you and was informed that it had been available to you in English, or was available to you in English, and in those circumstances we haven't re-copied it for you. I have got an English copy myself but I'm afraid I haven't got enough copies for all of you at the moment. We can make one more available, if that will help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we can have it back at the end so that our documents can be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Milosevic, if you have a particular passage, then bring that to the attention of the witness so that it can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Robinson, no specific passage is necessary here. Tab 24 shows that there is complete documentation pertaining to this person. It was compiled in Kosovo and Metohija. It contains the details of his burial. So the question is how can it be in the interest of any state organ to unearth man who was buried on the 5th of June, 1999, and rebury him in the north of Serbia? It makes no sense. Mr. Seselj just spoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that a question you're asking me? Because that would be an inversion of the process here. If you have a proper question to put to the witness on this point, then put it to him, but don't make a speech.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson, I will put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does this set of documents show, for example, that the state officially and in accordance with the regulations left precise traces as to when someone was killed, with all the necessary elements prescribed by the legislation?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the documentation of the government of Serbia, the Republic of Serbia, and the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, there has to be a multitude of documents that would show that we as a government on several occasions insisted with all police authorities that all corpses be treated with utmost care regardless of whether we are talking about terrorist casualties, killed terrorists in fighting, civilians killed in the bombing, et cetera, that all corpses should be dealt with in accordance with the law, that they should be buried properly, that every corpse be marked properly by a card with indestructible material containing all their particulars. That exists in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, just a few more concrete questions. This tab 24 has already been admitted. It gives a concrete example and I hope it's clear. You are from Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How often was this suburb bombed by NATO? Did you live in Batajnica throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent two-thirds of all those nights in Batajnica, and approximately every third night I was the duty deputy Prime Minister of the Republic of Serbia, and I was in the republican centre. Also following the NATO sorties. So I spent two-thirds of all those nights at my home in Batajnica. Batajnica was bombed every night, because one of our most important military airfields is in Batajnica. Along with the airfields, civilian buildings were bombed as well. There were many casualties. Among others, Milica Rakic, a three-year-old girl, was killed by an air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the training grounds of the special anti-terrorist police where those corpses were buried? I read about that in the newspapers when I was already in prison. And generally speaking, this centre of the anti-terrorist units, was it ever bombed during the NATO aggression?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre of the SAJ, of the special anti-terrorist unit, is at the very entrance into Batajnica. Throughout the war not a single bomb and not a single rocket hit that centre. The unit itself had been relocated before the bombing started. It was engaged the most in anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo and Metohija, but no one stayed behind at the centre. So the centre could have been targeted without involving a single casualty. However, the centre was never targeted. And in the yard of the centre, after the war and after the change of government, an enormous quantity of corpses was found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I'm asking you now in view of this great attention that was paid to Batajnica and the daily bombing of Batajnica and the fact that only this centre of the anti-terrorist unit was not bombed.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hospitals and schools were targeted in Belgrade because their suspicion was that soldiers were hidden there. That's what the NATO propagandists said. It is amazing, incredible that the centre of the anti-terrorist unit was not targeted. The empty building of the Ministry of Defence, the empty building of the General Staff was targeted, but the headquarters of one of our most important police units was never bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That part of the terrain, that is to say Batajnica including that centre, was the object of attention and surveillance. Was it possible for someone to bury hundreds of corpses in the training grounds of that elite police unit and NATO surveillance does not realise that at all?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was impossible because we were surveyed on a day-to-day basis. NATO could see every vehicle, everything in the country. AWACS were all over Serbia. We couldn't even speak over mobile phones. So we were under surveillance all the time of NATO. It was impossible for these corpses to be transported without filming the trucks that transported them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was the first time that you heard about some corpses from Kosovo and Metohija being transported to other parts of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first heard of that when it was published in the beginning of 2001. First, I made some statements perhaps these corpses were from the Second World War or from the Huns, their Emperor Atilla of the 6th century, he was fighting in the Panonian plain at that time. It was incredible. Why would this be done? What would be the motive for transporting corpses from Kosovo to the centre of the elite police unit? There is no motive. No one is in a position to indicate a motive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice claims that we did it in order to cover up purported crimes that, as he said here, the forces of the FRY and Serbia committed here.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we compiled complete documentation about different victims among the civilians, among the terrorists, bombing victims, et cetera. Complete documents, and then when we compile all these complete documents, then we hide corpses. What kind of an idiot would do that? Why would we conceal corpses? It is in our interest to have everything fully clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, wait a minute. There is not a single shred of evidence that has been presented by the regime until now that these were corpses of civilians, that this is the result of crimes, et cetera. Corpses were collected from different sites, brought in so that at a given moment, a favourable moment, they would be found in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Let us move on now to the next topic. In paragraph 16, it is stated that this so-called joint criminal enterprise that I took part in, and some other officials, as it says here, "other persons known and unknown," that it had the following objective, so 16 says that: "The purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was, inter alia, the expulsion of a substantial portion of the Kosovo Albanian population from the territory of the province of Kosovo in an effort to ensure continued Serbian control over the province." As the then deputy Prime Minister of the government of Serbia, do you know anything about this? Do you know about me or other officials or anybody in the authorities of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had that kind of an alleged purpose? Also, please answer the following question: Do you understand this explanation here that the objective was to ensure Serbian control over the province?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you answer, this is the kind of question that in the past you have answered in a very lengthy fashion. I want a specific answer. I want short answers. When you have given an answer that is short, then Mr. Milosevic comes back into the picture and asks another question. The first question he asked was whether you know anything of his involvement in the -- in this joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Robinson, you did not understand the question properly. I'm not talking about my participation. I'm asking him about whether he knew of any kind of joint criminal enterprise at all. How can somebody take part in an enterprise if the enterprise never existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, there was no criminal enterprise. There was no plan or intention to expel a considerable part of the Albanian population from Kosovo and Metohija. Even if there had been such an intention, what does that mean? You expel them today, you have to return them tomorrow. It was absolutely illogical to design such a plan. Thirdly, I first heard about this from the Washington Post in April --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speaker says 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when I read as deputy Prime Minister an article that refers to Action Horseshoe, and then it says that when General Clark was in Belgrade towards the end of 1988, Momcilo Perisic said to him that that was in the making, and we already knew at the time that Momcilo Perisic was a CIA agent, and he was removed a few days later. So it was the CIA that planted all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. You have given the answer. You did not know of any joint criminal enterprise as alleged in the indictment. What's the next question? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to add something,

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That had it existed by any chance, it would have been impossible, absolutely impossible for me not to know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, yes. We hear that as well. Next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 53, it says, and I quote to you: "After the joint criminal enterprise started, from the 1st of January, 1999, onwards, or around that date and continuing until the 20th of June, 1999, Slobodan Milosevic -" not to mention all the other names - "and others known and unknown, planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of terror and violence directed at Kosovo Albanian civilians living in Kosovo in the FRY." This kind of deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of violence could not have been carried out without the top echelons of government, including yourself, being informed about this. Tell me, was there such a campaign? Please give us your comments on what I've read out to you just now, what I quoted from number 53.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such a campaign. We had reliable information that Albanian terrorists resorted to various resources, propaganda, and intimidation in order to force the largest possible number of their own people to leave Kosovo, going to Macedonia or Albania. During the war, our forces intensified their anti-terrorist activities. Many Albanian terrorists changed into civilian clothing and used their own people who they had forced into being refugees, and they left our territory, mingling with the other refugees. We had information that in Albania they were being rearmed and involved in border skirmishes with our forces again. Our forces had strict authorities, first of all, to persuade the Albanian population not to move out. If they cannot persuade them not to move out, then they should ensure that their movement is safe, that they should not come across minefields. Also, they had instructions to help them by giving them food. Most often it was bread, but they did give them aid in food. Then to give them drinking water, medical assistance, and a few times it happened that columns of Albanians who were flooding towards the border were targeted by NATO Air Force and that is when they sustained a great many casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 55, it says: "The forces of the FRY of Serbia, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic manner, forcibly expelled and internally displaced hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians from their homes across the entire province of Kosovo. To facilitate these expulsions and displacements, forces of the FRY and Serbia intentionally created an atmosphere of fear and oppression through the use of force, threats of force, and acts of violence." So, to your knowledge as deputy Prime Minister, who I assume has to be active with regard to such matters, were there any expulsions? Were there any internal displacements of Kosovo Albanians, as is referred to in this quotation?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. There were no expulsions or displacements. There were individual incidents when certain soldiers or policemen tried to take advantage of the atmosphere of war, to loot, to steal things from these Albanians. And in these cases, our state authorities urgently intervened, and they practically prosecuted all these people. As far as I know, there are a couple of hundred such cases, and I think that they were all prosecuted. But the republican government, the federal government, the Ministry of Interior of Serbia gave instructions that all these cases should energetically be prosecuted and brought to justice. There were a great many trials of soldiers or policemen who had violated regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then the other part of this quotation, intimidation, threats of force, acts of violence, oppression, was there any such thing?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but by the Albanian terrorist organisation. When they could not persuade their own countrymen, civilians, to leave Kosovo and Metohija, there were even liquidations, killings, uses of threat of force and actual force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, in paragraph 56 of the Kosovo indictment, it says: "Throughout Kosovo, forces of the FRY and Serbia engaged in a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of destruction of property owned by Kosovo Albanian civilians. This was accomplished by the widespread shelling of towns and villages, the burning and destruction of property, including homes, farms, businesses, cultural monuments and religious sites, and the destruction of personal property. As a result of these orchestrated actions, villages, towns, and entire regions were made uninhabitable for Kosovo Albanians." I've finished the quotation, and I'm asking you, was there such a campaign of destroying property in the way mentioned here or in any other way? You as deputy Prime Minister of Serbia would have to know about that.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was absolutely no campaign whatsoever to destroy the property of Kosovo Albanians on the part of the government of Serbia or any other Serbian or FRY authorities. If partial destruction of property actually happened, then it could have only occurred in the legal, lawful clashes between the authorities and Albanian terrorists. But we need to compare what portion of Albanian property was destroyed by NATO action as opposed to the portion destroyed by our authorities in their struggle against the terrorists. I claim that much more property was destroyed by NATO bombs. On the other hand, if certain villages, towns, and whole areas became uninhabitable, then it was because -- because of NATO bombs containing depleted uranium. That is why certain places are uninhabitable. That is why to this day the soldiers who took part in this action keep dying of cancer. We can read about this in Italian press all the time. Also used were cluster bombs that are banned by international law of warfare. There are many such unexploded cluster bombs in Kosovo and Metohija and in central Serbia. After the war, we had cases of Albanian children dying because of those unexploded cluster bombs that they run across while playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that towns, villages, and entire areas in Kosovo and Metohija became uninhabitable for Serbs and other ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because survival became impossible for Serbs in every area where Albanians remained as a majority after the entry of the occupiers. Another proof of that is that hundreds of thousands of Albanians from Albania came to Kosovo and Metohija after the occupying forces entered Kosovo because life was better there. They would not leave Albania that had never been destroyed by war to go to Kosovo if there had not been a lot of property that they could seize, the property left behind by Serbs and other ethnic communities. That is the area that they filled in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that a lot of property was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, but by NATO bombing. You will see that in Pristina even the cemetery was bombed and skeletons flew about the place after NATO airstrikes. What kind of military target can you find in a cemetery?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the bombing of the centre of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, only on television, but it is abundant proof of the barbarian means used by the NATO alliance. I also saw the bombing of Belgrade every night by NATO rockets and bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 57 we read: "In addition to the deliberate destruction of property -" deliberate meaning intentional - "destruction of property owned by Kosovo Albanians, forces of the FRY and Serbia committed widespread or systematic acts of brutality and violence against Kosovo Albanian civilians in order to perpetuate the climate of fear, create chaos and a pervading fear for life. Forces of the FRY and Serbia went from village to village and, in the towns and cities, from area to area, threatening and expelling the Kosovo Albanian population. Kosovo Albanians were frequently intimidated, assaulted or killed in public view to enforce the departure of their families and neighbours." This is the end of -- of a quotation. Please do not think this is the way I speak Serbian, because this is pretty illiterate. "Many Kosovo Albanians who were not directly forcibly expelled from their communities fled as a result of the climate of terror created by the widespread or systematic beatings, harassment, sexual assaults, unlawful arrests, killings, shelling and looting carried out across the province. Forces of the FRY and Serbia persistently subjected Kosovo Albanians to insults, racial slurs, degrading acts and other forms of physical and psychological mistreatment based on their racial, religious and political identification. All sectors of Kosovo Albanian society were displaced, including women, children, the elderly, and the infirm." This is a rather long paragraph, 57. Now, please tell me - and you should be informed, in view of the posts you held - is it the case that the police and the army of our country actually carried out those widespread and systematic acts of violence against Kosovo Albanian civilians in order to perpetuate a climate of fear and a pervading fear of death?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolute fabrication. You have to look at the statistics about the number of Serb casualties and Albanian casualties during the NATO airstrikes. This is pure invention. I do not rule out the possibility of incidents, because there was the element of revenge. People recognised somebody as a relative of terrorists who had done something to their family, but those are lone cases that cannot be, should not be generalised. But the total numbers of casualties speak very clearly that the situation was not like some tried to represent it. After so much bombing and so much terrorist and anti-terrorist action, there was an improbably low number of casualties among Albanian civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Time for the 20-minute break. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, is it true that, as it says in this paragraph 57, many Kosovo Albanians fled because of the climate of terror created by widespread and systematic beatings, harassment, sexual assaults, unlawful arrests, killings, shellings, and looting?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. The main reason for this mass movement of Albanians was the bombing. And it made not only Albanians flee; it had the same effect on Serbs, Romas, Goranis, et cetera. Second, a great part of Albanians did not rush for Albania. They went to Serbia, Macedonia, and Montenegro. They were fleeing American bombs and rockets. Also, the Albania terrorist organisation led a campaign to force their own civilians to leave Kosovo and Metohija. They distributed a huge number of leaflets to civilians which contained threats and incentives, all in order to make them leave their homes. We are in possession of a great number of these leaflets. We did not, therefore, lead a policy of persecution and expulsion but tried instead to persuade the Albanian population not to go. We were mainly unsuccessful because the fear of the bombing was too great. And as I said, there were individual incidents and there were individual policemen and soldiers with dishonourable intentions. Maybe there were some sexual assaults. We in the government of Serbia did not have such information. But in any case, we gave strict instructions to state authorities to prosecute all cases of flagrant violation of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said Albanians were fleeing, Serbs were fleeing. Could you tell us on a very general level, why did Albanians flee and why did Serbs and others flee?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Milosevic, that I live in Batajnica. The main reason was the same. Even I put my family up with my in-laws. I didn't want my children exposed directly to the bombs, and I thought my house could become a target just as yours did. If there had been an atmosphere of fear created by us, it would have been evident before the bombing, but it wasn't there. In all Kosovo towns the atmosphere was peaceful. It was even idyllic, I could say. There were no incidents in towns. Incidents happened in villages where Albanian terrorists were active. Just before the bombing, all roads in Kosovo and Metohija were completely passable and free. Not a single road was cut off by the terrorists. It was to that extent that our police were successful in suppressing terrorism. You know that in 1998 you couldn't go through from Pec through Drenica to Pristina. Here in prison, another accused, Limaj, told me that they had heard my statement on the radio and organised an ambush on the road that goes through Drenica. Of course I took another road and they missed me. But before the war, all the roads were passable. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there anybody creating an atmosphere of terror?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was the Albanian terrorist organisation the KLA. They killed many of their own compatriots whom they suspected of being loyal to Serb authorities all because those people did not obey their orders to leave their homes and go God knows where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, as it says in this paragraph, that Kosovo Albanians were constantly exposed to insults, racial slurs, degrading acts and other forms of physical and psychological mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such thing on the part of the authorities certainly. Incidents happened, sometimes involving civilians. Look, just before the war Albanian terrorists threw a bomb at a cafe in Pec which was a gathering point for Serb high-school students. These activities certainly deepened ethnic or inter-ethnic mistrust. There was a large dose of inter-ethnic mistrust but there was no organised activity of this kind that you mentioned here, especially not organised by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to paragraph 58.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just tell me which tab it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I mean this so-called indictment, paragraph 58. Do you have it here?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it with me, but I can follow you very carefully. It's not a problem, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope somebody can provide you with a copy so you have it in front of you, but I will quote, in any case, paragraph 58. It says: "Thousands of Kosovo Albanians who fled their homes as a result of the conduct of the forces of the FRY and Serbia and the deliberate climate of terror that pervaded the territory of Kosovo joined convoys of persons that moved towards Kosovo's borders with the Republic of Albania and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. Along the routes to the border crossings, forces of the FRY and Serbia manned checkpoints where the displaced Kosovo Albanians were subject to further beatings, extortion, robbery, harassment, assaults, illegal arrests, and killings. At other times forces of the FRY and Serbia escorted groups of expelled Kosovo Albanians to the borders. By these methods, the forces of the FRY and Serbia maintained control over the movement of displaced Kosovo Albanians to the borders. Displaced Kosovo Albanians often arrived at the borders of Kosovo on foot, in convoys of several thousand persons, or carried by tractors, trailers and trucks, as well as on trains, buses or trucks which were organised and provided by the forces of the FRY and Serbia." Is it the case that Albanians who went to Macedonia and Albania were forced to do so by the forces of FRY and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no terror perpetrated by the authorities. Whenever we failed to persuade Albanians to stay in their homes, then we tried to help them. If we were trying to instil fear, why would we distribute thousands of loaves of bread to those Albanians who were forced by the terrorists to leave? Why would we be organising water supply to them? Those convoys of Albanians that were moving towards border crossings were really creating a huge problem to our authorities. Nevertheless, we tried to help them. Means of transportation were provided to them at their request. I don't know of a single case when a tractor or a trailer was taken away from them. There were certain individuals who took advantage of those unfortunate people to rob them, but those individuals were arrested by the police, and it was in such cases that some harassment occurred. But look at how many people travelling in these convoys were killed by NATO bombs and how many were killed in such incidents. The difference in numbers is huge. So this theory from the indictment absolutely does not stand up to scrutiny. Where are the figures to support it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how about the passage that I quoted to you where it says that at checkpoints manned by the forces of FRY and Serbia displaced Kosovo Albanians were subjected to further beatings, extortion, robbery, harassment, assaults, illegal arrests and killings.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just try to imagine that. Hundreds of thousands of Albanians were moving in those convoys, and now somebody standing at a checkpoint, stopping them in order to beat them and harass them. Do you know what it means to stop such a convoy? Do you know it from rallies when we tried to keep order and to avoid sudden movements of those masses? Now, can you visualise those hundreds of thousands of Albanians moving and our police stopping them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I sincerely hope that your evidence from Mr. Seselj on other matters will be different from the evidence that we have heard so far. So far there is nothing in his testimony, in my view, that assists your case. All he's doing is giving a general comment on passages in the indictment. The other witnesses that you have called, some of them have information, albeit hearsay, but they have information about incidents in the indictment. All Mr. Seselj is doing is saying how incredible the allegations are. That's a matter that you can comment on. In fact, I even wonder whether evidence of this nature is a proper use of the Tribunal's time, and it's a matter that I will raise with my colleagues during the next break. I thought Mr. Seselj had specific information about some of the matters in the indictment. Take, for example, his last answer. He hasn't said anything at all. He's just raising a question as to whether the allegations in the indictment could have taken place in the manner set out in the indictment. He finds it incredulous, but that doesn't help your case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it's correct that these are general questions, but they pertain to general counts in the indictment, to allegations that there was some kind of joint criminal enterprise, some kind of plan, some sort of -- and I quote here. I'm quoting from what Mr. Nice and his office, and Mrs. Del Ponte wrote. They say that there was some sort of plan, some sort of joint criminal enterprise, and here we have a deputy Prime Minister, the president of the Serb Radical Party, who would have had to know about such a plan. He would have known had there been a plan. And he is testifying that this is not true, that what I'm quoting is completely untrue, and that's the case. Things have been turned upside down here. Mr. Nice has not put forward a single shred of evidence as to the existence of a plan except for the so-called Horseshoe Plan, and that's nonsense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can't say that it is irrelevant because it does relate to the matters in the indictment, but I really question whether this is the best use of the time that is available to you. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Nice wishes to withdraw his allegation about a joint criminal enterprise, then I don't have to put these general questions. But as far as I was able to understand, due to a lack of evidence, there was this phantom joint criminal enterprise that was invented, and the intention of the Serbian authorities to expel the Albanians and kill them. I'm quoting from what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, did the army, the police, and the civilian authorities try to influence the Albanians not to leave their homes and not to leave the country?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: By what means? What means did they use to try to influence the Albanians to stay?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persuasion and offering material aid, providing guarantees of safety and promising them that they would be protected by our police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serb authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, stop. Now, that's a pertinent question. That's a matter that is in dispute. So let us find out from him the basis for the information that he has. Mr. Seselj, what is the basis for the answer that you just gave to Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, we had almost daily sessions of the cabinet. At least three times a week I had meetings with Mr. Milosevic during the bombing. I was directly familiar with everything that was taking place in Kosovo and Metohija, and I participated in the creation of these events, in the creation of the government policy. Without the Serbian government, nobody could have done anything down there without the government knowing about it. It was the policy of the Serbian government to dissuade the Albanians from leaving Kosovo and Metohija.
