The Serb government policy was to protect the Albanians, both from the terrorists and from the NATO pact. On the other hand, there was fear among us. If a terrorist organisation was moving all the Albanians out of Kosovo and Metohija, then the NATO bombing would be even worse. Why would we want to be left without a civilian population in Kosovo and Metohija? We needed a civilian population there. The territory had to be inhabited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what it seems to me we need is specific examples. If there was persuasion, if material aid was offered, if there were guarantees of safety, if they were promised that they would be protected by the police and army, then it's concrete examples of these that would assist the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm telling you about specific examples. The interim Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija was constantly out on the ground. I was in charge of the economy and finances, and I know that we gave enormous material aid to the population there regardless of their ethnic affiliation. Enormous funds were set aside for this purpose, and this was distributed on the ground. All the resources of a government serve this purpose. And if we were unable to persuade them to stay, what else could we do but assist them to reach the border in safety?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's absolutely no factual content in the answer you've just given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is based on facts. And as for documentation, you have it available in the archives of the interim Executive Council of Kosovo and Metohija. It would be very easy for you to gain access to it. I cannot do that because I'm in prison. My hands are tied. I'm telling you about the facts, and these facts have been documented. The documents are in the archives of the Serbian government and of the interim Executive Council of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, we are not running the Defence of the accused. The Chamber is not running the Defence of the accused. If he has information, then it is for the accused. It is for him to get the information and present it before the Court. It's not for the Court to get the information. Next question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I am not here to defend the accused. I came here at the request of the accused to testify to events as I know them and according to my participation in them. It is my wish and intention to tell the truth. If what I say does not fit into the case either of the accused or the Prosecution, well that's nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I've stopped you. What would be helpful is when you provide an answer to the accused, let us know the basis, the source of the information. If you got it from somebody who worked with you, a subordinate, then say so, because that makes the evidence more credible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No more of that. Next question. Mr. Milosevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, in connection to what you said, you probably don't remember that there was a large number of witnesses through which -- through whom we introduced the evidence Mr. Seselj is referring to. He is testifying about his own experience and his own activity in the government in connection with these events and this conduct. For example, Vukasin Andric testified here. He was the secretary for health in Kosovo and he showed films about the assistance and the aid distributed to the displaced Albanians, about how efforts were made to persuade them to return home, how there was no discrimination when aid was being distributed, and so on and so forth. You saw many orders during the testimony of General Stevanovic. You heard the testimony of General Delic about the assistance offered to the population by the army. Mr. Seselj is speaking about the conduct of the government, and you have already had witnesses providing specific evidence as to behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I understand you to be saying that his evidence is by way of confirming other evidence that has been given by some of your witnesses, but the manner in which he's giving it, in my view, does not add much to that evidence. I question whether it adds to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that evidence at all, because he's merely making general statements without providing any -- any basis for the information that he says that he has received. And Mr. Nice no doubt will question him on those matters. Yes, next question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The authorities attempted, as you said, to persuade Albanians to provide them with humanitarian aid and so on and so forth. Did the authorities of Serbia and Yugoslavia try to prevent anyone, including Albanians, from leaving Kosovo and Metohija by force?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they would not have been allowed to do that under our constitution and our legislation. Freedom of movement was guaranteed, and no one had any legal basis to forcibly prevent this. On the other hand, when this huge convoy appeared, it was impossible to stop them. The problem would only have been made worse. To stop people on the roads - they would have been there in large groups, the concentration of people would have built up - and what would have happened? It was impossible to control this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The authorities did not prevent this, which is logical. Did they provide means of transport?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever it was necessary and whenever the government was able to do so, it provided means of transportation, especially for women, children, the elderly, the sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Only for the Albanians or for others?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For everyone, whoever needed that. We had cases where our authorities provided transport for a group of Serb civilians and civilians of other ethnicities, and they were all killed in the bombing. They were of various ethnic origins, but most of them were Serbs. We have seen that NATO bombed a passenger train.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that this passenger train was not intended specifically for Serbs or Albanians but for all citizens.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We never checked the ethnic affiliation of citizens entering trains or buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this alleged expulsion of Albanians, the alleged persecution of Albanians, during the cross-examination of Professor Ratko Markovic, Mr. Nice played an excerpt from a speech you made in Zemun on the 27th of February, 1999, for the Serb Radical Party. This was a brief excerpt where you said that if there is NATO bombing and if there is American aggression, we Serbs will suffer greatly, but there will be no Albanians on Kosovo any more. Would you please explain what you meant by those words. And I will ask you especially to explain the context in which you said this.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I handed over to you the text of the entire speech. First of all, it makes no sense to pull a few sentences out of the context of a long speech. You can see from the speech that everything said there was intended to dissuade potential aggressors, to deter aggression. I know that where the Americans helped Muslims, Croats, or others, it was mostly the population in question that died. Where Americans bombed from planes, there has always been large-scale killing of civilians. And I was bearing in mind the case in Hadzici where the Americans were bombing Republika Srpska, used the bombs with depleted uranium. After the Dayton agreement, the population of Hadzici moved to Bratunac, and many of them immediately began to die. There was a real epidemic of cancer caused by this depleted uranium. And you can see now how the Americans have affected the Albanians, especially in those areas targeted with depleted uranium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am having trouble following the way in which or the degree to which the answer is responsive to the question. While I'm on my feet, if there is a full version of the speech, it may well be available to us in another way, if it's been provided to the accused, perhaps it could also be provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand the witness to be saying, Mr. Nice, that you took out of context the passage that was put. I also understand him to be saying that, in his experience, where Americans had helped Muslims and Croats, it was mostly the population in question that died. And I understand that he is saying in effect that his speech -- in his speech what he meant was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Fine. Can we have a copy in full?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That they would -- let me finish. What he meant was that Kosovo Albanians would suffer as a result of aggression and not as a result of action by the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the problem with that -- the problem is that the words are, and he was asked to define these words, "There will be no Albanians on Kosovo any more," and I so far haven't been assisted by the explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, in light of the controversy -- let me finish. Let me ask you to say exactly what you meant by the phrase, "There will be no Albanians in Kosovo any more."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before Mr. Seselj answers your question, as this comes in the middle of my series of questions about what Mr. Nice said here, let me draw your attention to the fact that in tab 30 you have the whole text of this speech, the entire speech where Mr. Nice pulled out half a sentence out of context. Secondly, in tab 30 you also have a complete English translation of this speech which Mr. Nice is asking to see, and it is included in these documents. Tab 30, then, contains both a photocopy from the special edition of Velika Srbija where this speech was printed and the English translation done by your service here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, thanks for that information. It's in tab 30. Now, Mr. Seselj, answer the question. What did you mean by the phrase "There will be no Albanians ... any more"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant, first of all, that because of the consequences of the bombing, they would suffer grievously. Secondly, I was bearing in mind that their mass exodus was being prepared under the control of the Albanian terrorist organisation. The only threat I made in this entire speech was against those Albanians who were disloyal and cooperating with the Albanian terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm stopping you for a minute to ask you to point to passages in the speech that support your conclusion as to the meaning to be attributed to that statement that it was the bombing that would result in no more Albanians being in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the whole speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, don't say the whole speech. That's not helpful at all. You say that it was taken out of context. Then point to a passage in the speech that puts it in context, that makes more credible your statement that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'll read that passage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. The interpreters are asking for a copy of the speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot look at it in English. I can't find it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... provide.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 11 of the Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the interpreters need a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have a copy and have found the reference. It's on page 4. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed now. What is the passage to which you are directing our attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the first passage of the third column on page 11 of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just say how it begins so we can try to find it in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "We Serbs are a people with a marked democratic tradition --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us try to find it in the English text.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The bottom of page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "We have ideological differences, we have political differences, we have all sorts of differences, but when the homeland is at stake, there are no differences. We yet have to see a Serb ready to sign approval for foreign troops to come to our territory, we have yet to see a Serb ready to sign the separation of Kosovo and Metohija from the legal system of Serbia. We, Serbs, as a democratic people, have offered the Albanians time and again the highest level of autonomy, of cultural autonomy, for them to live as loyal citizens, for them to regulate their own school, health, information systems, and so on. They do not want that. The only thing they want is secession, and they are unable to secede unaided. They are aware of that, so they are reckoning - the Americans will fight a winning battle for them in the Balkans. From this place I say to them, and this is not only a message from the Serbian Radical Party, I'm convinced of that, it is a message from the entire Serbian nation: The Albanians will have a chance only if they opt for a peaceful, democratic, political way of dialogue." I'm trying to avert aggression and I'm calling for a democratic settlement to the dispute. And then another sentence: "In the event of a NATO bombardment, in the event of an American aggression, we Serbs shall perish in quite large numbers, but there will be no Albanians in Kosovo!" I'm simply expecting Kosovo to be the main theatre of war. We are going to defend Kosovo with major military equipment. Without bombing Kosovo with their bombs, Americans cannot take Kosovo. And who is going to suffer the most? Those who are the majority population. And then I say: "Surely the Americans do not believe that if they attack us we will allow armed bands and disloyal citizens behind our backs who can hardly wait to stab us in the back." So who is not loyal? Those who support terrorists. And any aiding and abetting of terrorism is a crime according to our law, and even those who are giving aid and food to terrorists are committing a crime, according to our law. And then I warn neighbouring states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Seselj. I think that you quoted this quite correctly. However, I would like to ask you to quote yet another part. This is on the last page of the transcript of this speech or, rather, the photocopy of the newspaper where this was presented. It starts in the middle paragraph, at the very end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for you gentlemen it is on page 6, the third or fourth paragraph from the top. It starts with the following words: "We Serbs do not want war."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You end with this, so could you please read your own speech so I don't read it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say in that speech: "We Serbs do not want war. We Serbs never wanted war. We Serbs have not set out to conquer the territories of others for a thousand years, we only defended what is ours and we managed to defend most of the Serbian lands with utmost effort and difficulty. We shall never renounce restoring what has been temporarily occupied. That is a pledge of the Serbian Radicals that cannot be departed from."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the following paragraph, I consider that to be important too: "Now, when we are weighed down by the burden of economic crisis and social poverty, when we should focus on addressing our internal problems, they are again beating the war drums --"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... and sounding the war bugles in the West. New attacks are in the making. They are building up troops and wondering how come Serbia is not scared and how come Serbia is getting ready for a defence. They have satellite imagery. They can see it. Well, of course Serbia is getting ready to defend itself, because Serbia is a state worthy of defending and Serbia has not --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, we have heard enough from that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just the highlight when the microphone was turned off: "And we are going to do everything we can in order to avert war, but if there is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. war imposed on us, we shall have no option but to fight."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is the speech that Mr. Nice used in order to show that it was against Albanians. Is any further comment needed in addition to what we've already quoted, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the entire speech was aimed at averting aggression. I would even say that it was a desperate attempt to avert the aggressor who was already ready and who could strike any moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us move on. You have paragraph 59, which says, and I'm going to quote it: "In addition, thousands of Kosovo Albanians who fled their homes --" I hope you have received a copy of this blue book.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they're persistent in not giving it to me but I'm listening to you carefully and I can remember. Just tell me what's the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you sit down? Can you not stand behind my back? It has a bad psychological effect on me. I'm not a dangerous man. There is no need for you to stand behind my back. Just sit down, will you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The usher is there for a purpose and he will remain there. Your comment is entirely out of order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I withdraw my comment, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you read paragraph 59 out yourself.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In addition, thousands of Kosovo Albanians who fled their homes and were thereby forcibly transferred as a result of the conduct of the forces of the FRY and Serbia and the deliberate climate of terror that pervaded the territory of Kosovo, were forced to seek shelter for days, weeks, or months in other towns and villages and/or in forests and mountains throughout the province. Some of these internally displaced persons remained inside the province of Kosovo throughout the time period relevant to this indictment, and many persons died as a consequence of the harsh weather conditions, insufficient food, inadequate medical attention, and exhaustion. Others eventually crossed over one of the Kosovo borders into Albania, Macedonia, Montenegro, or crossed the provincial boundary between Kosovo and Serbia. Forces of the FRY and Serbia controlled and coordinated the movements of many internally displaced Kosovo Albanians until they were finally expelled from Kosovo." Well, in the indictment it is admitted that many of these Albanians went into Serbia, and Montenegro is within the same state. So their only objective was to get away from where the NATO airstrikes were the strongest or where they were being jeopardised by terrorists. And it is due to those circumstances that they moved to the areas where the war operations were lesser, and that will happen in any part anywhere in this world of yours. It is quite inappropriate to mention some kind of climate of terror or torture or forcible expulsions or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would like the Court to note where it has reached. The witness is being invited to read out and then to comment on passages of the indictment pretty well freely. It doesn't match Your Honour's general expectation that questions should be focused and answers should be brief, and I would forecast that this is not a pattern of examination that the Chamber would want to repeat, either with this witness or with others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, I've already made it clear that the Chamber has clear predilection for short answers in response to short and direct specific questions that relate to the issues raised by the indictment, and let us follow that course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, in order to be able to put a short question, I would have to have a short quotation. Unfortunately, you see that this which Mr. Nice has honoured with the name of indictment, time and again there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm cutting you off. Just follow the direction. I'm not allowing a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you read half a page, and that is paragraph 59. Did the internally displaced persons leave their homes because of terror and because of being forced out by our forces or our authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A categorical no. It was either due to the NATO Air Force or pressure by the Albanian terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have spoken about our attitude toward the civilian population; Albanian, Serb, and of all other ethnicities. You have spoken about the need to help them, how they were helped, what the government policy was, and what the government did in this context. Since an objection was raised that you had to document it further, please give me answers to the following few questions: Since you were a deputy Prime Minister, you know how it functioned, does a government pass general decisions or does it deal with concrete situations in every village, in every hamlet, or in any territory in particular?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, a government passes general decisions. However, in order to pass these general decisions, it has to be very familiar with the situation and the most important details comprising that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How was this spelled out in concrete terms, these government decisions? Were you regularly informed about the implementation of government decisions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had daily reports about everything that happened in Kosovo and Metohija and all the problems encountered by the local authorities, either the local self-government or the local posts of the central government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph -- in paragraph 60, it says, and I hope you can see it, I hope it follows immediately after paragraph 59: "Throughout Kosovo, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic effort to deter expelled Kosovo Albanians from returning --" this is very strange Serbian. The language is very strange. "... from returning to their homes, the forces of the FRY and Serbia looted and pillaged the personal and commercial property belonging to Kosovo Albanians. Forces of the FRY and Serbia used wholesale searches, threats of force, and acts of violence to rob Kosovo Albanians of money and valuables, and in a widespread or systematic manner, authorities at FRY border posts stole personal vehicles and other property from Kosovo Albanians being deported from the province." I am sorry. It looks as if I were putting the same question all the time, but if you look at it you will see that these are all different paragraphs in the same document. I keep repeating the paragraphs of what is called an indictment here, and does the deputy Prime Minister have to know about all these things? Did you have any knowledge about widespread, systematic lootings and other such things mentioned in paragraph 60?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The forces of the FRY and Serbia did not loot and steal. If there were cases of looting, these were individual incidents, and in every case the state authorities reacted. They prevented this or held the perpetrators answerable before law. There is hardly a single case that went by unpunished. I've already said that several hundred cases were prosecuted of crimes committed there; killings, lootings, theft, and so on. So our forces did not do that in an organised fashion. They did not do it at all. But there were individual cases that even members of those forces did that sometimes, but the state authorities reacted in each and every case, and that is documented in the state archives. All crimes were prosecuted, those committed during the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a great deal of evidence has been presented about that. So if I put this question to you: Were there cases where the members of the military and the police or other persons that looted and stole from Albanians in Kosovo, on the basis of what you're saying now, the answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there's no doubt about that. No one can deny, but these are only individual cases, but almost all such cases have been prosecuted. Perhaps there were some omissions, but very few. A vast majority were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So can this be referred to as systematic and widespread crimes?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is nonsense, and I categorically claim that there was no organised looting and stealing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the authorities reacted to these crimes, all the authorities from the lowest level to the highest level?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were always arrests, investigations, and criminal reports, regardless of whether these were soldiers or policemen or civilians. Several hundred such cases were dealt with, were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In 61, it says -- or, rather, read it out yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In addition, throughout Kosovo, forces of the FRY and Serbia systematically seized and destroyed the personal identity documents and licenses of vehicles belonging to Kosovo Albanian civilians. As Kosovo Albanians were forced from their homes and directed towards Kosovo's borders, they were subjected to demands to surrender identity documents at selected points en route to border crossings and at border crossings into Albania and Macedonia. These actions were undertaken in order to erase any record of the deported Kosovo Albanians' presence in Kosovo and to deny them the right to return to their homes." There was one single case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I predict you will say nothing like that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, your assumption is wrong, Mr. Robinson. I want to confirm something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one single such case happened, at the border crossing near Prizren, where the police organs, individuals among the police at the border crossing demanded from the Albanians that they hand over their personal identity documents when crossing the border. When the chief of police in Prizren found out about this, he immediately reacted and prevented this from happening again. As for the consequences of taking these documents away, they certainly could not have been as mentioned in the indictment here because in Serbia there are centralised records, computerised records for the entire republic. There are books, registers. If any Albanian, like any other citizen, loses his documents, he can get them again. He can get new copies from the central computer. There is not a single shred of evidence stating that we intervened from the centralised computer by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I recognise that you normally speak at a high level, but there are times when I'm convinced that you are shouting. Don't get excited.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not true. I'm not excited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Try to speak a little more softly because the high decibel level interferes with the transmission of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, maybe you could turn down the volume in your headset or you can organise an examination by a doctor, and you will see that my blood pressure is normal, my pulse is normal, and I'm not excited. I speak the way I'm speaking now ever since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem is it's your volume we need to turn down, not our volume. And we would be greatly assisted, as would the presentation of evidence, if you could try to tone your voice down slightly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, when you say one case, you don't mean a case involving one person whose documents were taken away; you mean one case of a single border crossing when it happened.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the exact number involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you say that when the chief of police of Prizren heard about it --

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intervened and put a stop to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Put a stop to it. You explained that it wouldn't matter anyway because there is a central computerised system of personal data, and we heard that from General Stevanovic as well. We will not dwell on it any more. Now, there are many paragraphs in the indictment. One of them will take us to an earlier period. Please read paragraph 75.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During the 1980s, Serbs voiced concern about discrimination against them by the Kosovo Albanian-led provincial government while Kosovo Albanians voiced concern about economic underdevelopment and called for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. greater political liberalisation and republican status for Kosovo. From 1981 onwards, Kosovo Albanians staged demonstrations, which were suppressed by SFRY military and police forces of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. Now, will you answer this: Is it the case that during the 1980s, Kosovo Albanians voiced concern about discrimination they were exposed to from the Kosovo leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Is it the case that Serbs voiced concern about being discriminated against by the Kosovo leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs were exposed not only to discrimination but to systematic persecution and expulsions by the Provincial Government, and that was attested to by the leadership or members of the leadership from other republics who came to visit; Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, et cetera. On the other hand, Kosovo has the fastest economic development from 1945 until 1990, and the entire Yugoslavia set aside special funds into a fund for the development of Kosovo and Metohija. You should compare the economic development of Kosovo with that of Albania, using the period before the Second World War as a baseline. I think that during those several decades the economic development of Kosovo was the fastest in Europe. Second, not a single Albanian party asked for economic liberalisation. From 1981 to 1990 Kosovo Albanians formed exclusively Stalinist, Marxist-Leninist parties and it is impossible to expect such parties to voice demands for economic liberalisation. Our military and the police suppressed only violent demonstrations, whereas peaceful demonstrations that were conducted in keeping with the law, and we had a law on public gatherings, were never suppressed by anybody. The only ones to be suppressed were violent demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Regarding this paragraph 75 to which you answered covering several points about what they voiced concern over, among other things you said whether it was true or not that Kosovo Albanians voiced concern about economic underdevelopment and called for greater liberalisation. I wish to return to that article written by Mr. Kristan. I hope you still have it.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at what he wrote in 1981, because this paragraph 75 speaks about the situation that prevailed during the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 1731. Will you please just quote the fourth paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This passage in paragraph 4, where it says: "Regarding the claim that Albanians in Yugoslavia are not equal..."

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, put it on the ELMO and read it from the ELMO, just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Regarding the claim that they are not equal, that they are oppressed as a nation, one can only say that it is an example of nationalist and political propaganda."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's enough. So what they say in paragraph 75 is qualified by Kristan as an example of nationalist propaganda, hostile nationalist propaganda.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but in order for the Trial Chamber to understand, we have to mention here that Kristan later became one of the main proponents of ideological separatism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not essential. But the essence of paragraph 75 is qualified by Kristan as propaganda. He says it is an example of hostile nationalist propaganda. Now, turn the page and read from paragraphs 2 and 3 on page 1732.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Regarding the demand for Albanians to get a state, that is a republic, instead of autonomy, the slogan 'Kosovo Republic' is revolutionary and hostile because its objective is to upset the constitutional order of Yugoslavia, to change its borders, and to achieve annexation to Albania. Why does propaganda from Albania insist that Kosovo has to become a republic? Of course every nation has interest to have which state, not two. The same goes for Albania and Kosovo. We see why when we look at the demand for Kosovo to secede. It is only the first step towards its annexation towards Albania. We can read that from the Albanian daily Zere [phoen] and Popullit, which says that there was discussion about all topics except one, and that one topic was annexation of Kosovo to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was the ultimate purpose of achieving the status of republic for Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secession and later annexation to Albania, because according to the Yugoslav constitution, republics were set up as states, although we had a federal state. But this state was made up not of units that had statehood to begin with; it was made up of units that formed a state. And if somebody had a status of republic, then it was implied that through the principle of self-determination, they would have the right to secede and ultimately become a part of something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You see on page 1736 Kristan suggests in the last paragraph: "The leading idea in all this has to be the preservation of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the consolidation of its internal strengths and international reputation." That's what Kristan writes. So it was obvious for everybody at the time where the solution lies, and those who orchestrated the war in the former Yugoslavia tried to destroy precisely that. Is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're moving into a kind of debate where the accused is advancing his propositions again. It's not question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the precise objection, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, a question that says, "So it was obvious for everybody at the time that the situation lies, and those who orchestrated the ..." We move imperceptibly to that kind of proposition partly because it's very difficult to follow the evidence and I suspect concentration lapses, but there it is. It shouldn't be a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, just reformulate that question. It's leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice frequently makes a speech ending it with "Isn't it?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "So it was obvious for everybody at the time," et cetera; that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. No leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will just repeat this quotation, and without any leading questions, I want your answer. "The leading idea in clearing up these relations has to be the preservation of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the consolidation of its internal strength and international reputation." Was that the prevailing position in Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All political elites in all federal units held that position all the way until 1989; that is, for a full five years after those anti-state violent demonstrations broke out in Pristina which led to the engagement to army and police units from all federal units, not only from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anything -- could anything that happened in Kosovo or in Serbia lead other federal units to change their opinion suddenly?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They could only change their position following the dictat from the West when the action to break up Yugoslavia began.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We heard another witness here, Mr. Ibrahim Rugova. He stated that I did not want a political solution to Kosovo but that I wanted instead a war for the next ten years with the intention of expelling the population.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there was no expulsion of Albanian population from Kosovo. The number of Albanians constantly rose. It didn't drop. Second, you constantly tabled initiatives to find a solution and an agreement about this problem. And with the mediation of some Vatican organisation, you did reach an agreement with Rugova in 1995, and that agreement that concerns schooling was in fact implemented. The state provided several buildings for Albanians to set up their own schools and universities because they did not wish to attend the existing ones. There was no limit to the number of students; they were absolutely free to run those schools. Nobody questioned the right of Albanians to express their individuality and their collective consciousness as long as it all fell short of jeopardising the integrity of Serbia. Anything else could be a matter for discussion and was a matter for discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand your answer. Thank you for that answer. Now, regarding his assertions that violence became ever-worse, with the intention to expel them from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For your benefit, gentlemen, it is on page 4982 of the transcript of the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Rugova also stated that in Rambouillet there was no willingness to negotiate on the Serbian side. "[In English] Was the LDK delegation serious in its attempts to negotiate or not?" [Interpretation] I am now reading from the transcript which is, unfortunately, provided only in English. "Yes, we were serious," is the answer, [In English] "and we went in with the conviction that an agreement must be achieved. And this was the stand of the international community too, after the massacre at Racak. The situation was deteriorating in Kosova. And of course the Kosova delegation consisted mainly of the LDK, including myself and other political groups. There was the movement for democratic unity, and the KLA, and other civil societies, and there were two other members. So there were about 15 members in this team. So the other key position was that an agreement --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking you to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you heard what Rugova said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not correct, because in Rambouillet there was not a single meeting that was actually held between the delegation of Albanians and the delegation of the government of the Republic of Serbia. Not a single meeting, because the Albanians were resolute in their refusal to hold it. How can there be dialogue between sides if it is never started? We could never meet. We kept asking to meet them, and they were persistent in refusing to talk. There was not a single meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You see what he says, speaking about the Serbian side. He says most of them were not serious. "[In English] It appeared to me that they were not there in order to reach some agreement. That was our impression, given the way the talks were being held, or the process, in fact. Because we didn't have many contacts, but these negotiations -- the process continued for three weeks and we didn't see any willingness on their part to reach some agreement." [Interpretation] He says there was not much contact. Was there any contact at all?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no contact and that's why they couldn't see anything. They even avoided casual, accidental contact during walks in the yard in Rambouillet. How could we achieve anything if they kept running away from talk? All positions can be only expressed during dialogue. They kept avoiding to meet us and surmising what our position could have been, whereas on our side there was willingness to discuss everything as long as the territorial integrity of our country was not jeopardised. We were prepared to talk about any form of autonomy that existed in the world, not only from the viewpoint of international law, but we were even willing to look at making a precedent leaning towards greater autonomy and greater rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, remind me, were you there throughout the Rambouillet arrangements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We, the Serb Radicals, had our standpoint, and it was that these talks were a manipulation by the Western forces and that they would yield no results. We told our coalition partners this in advance, but as members of the government, we did not oppose the forming of this delegation. However, there was no member of the Serb Radical Party in the delegation because we simply did not trust the Americans or the other Western forces. We knew that they would lie to us, manipulate us, try to trick us, but we did not oppose this attempt as a final attempt to avoid war. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. It's time for the 20-minute break. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I have observed that you do not stand when the Chamber enters and leaves the courtroom. I will hear from you, but I am bound to say that this appears to be disrespectful not only to the Chamber but to the International Tribunal as a whole. A witness who comes to give evidence here must abide by the Rules, the conventions, and the protocols of the Tribunal. One course that is open to the Tribunal, if you maintain this and there is no acceptable explanation, is that the Chamber will not hear any more evidence from you. Let me hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I am aware that it is the practice of this International Tribunal for a witness to address the Chamber sitting. Secondly, I have read all the Rules and all the documents of the Tribunal put at my disposal, and nowhere have I read that either the accused or a witness has to rise when the Chamber enters, the Trial Chamber enters. The third reason is of a religious nature. I was told by priests of the Serb Orthodox Church before arriving here that the uniforms worn by the Judges here resemble the uniform worn by the former Catholic Inquisition, and this is something I do not respect. The way you bow when you enter the courtroom reminds me of a satanic ritual. I have tried to find a para-psychological explanation for this. I'm afraid that should I bow to your ceremonial, my consciousness might be affected by forces I cannot control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me deal with the three explanations that you have given. You say that it is the practice of the Tribunal for a witness to address the Chamber sitting. We are not dealing with that. You can sit when you address the Chamber. The situation we are dealing with is the convention, the practice, the protocol of everybody rising when the Chamber enters the room. You say that you have not read anywhere where this is required. This is a protocol. It is a convention, and you hear the usher say words to the effect "All rise." You are to abide by it. The third reason that you give I reject entirely. That is nonsense. So you think it over and decide what you are going to do, and it's a matter that affects the interests of Mr. Milosevic. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, under your threat that you will sanction my failure to rise by interrupting my testimony, in future I will rise, but only before this particular Trial Chamber. Under this threat that you will bring my testimony to an end, I will rise when you enter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milosevic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was turned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, Knut Vollebaek testified here, the Norwegian minister of foreign affairs, who at the time when the Verification Mission was established and at the time of the crisis in Kosovo was chairing the OSCE. He stated here that at one of our meetings I told him about my commitment to a multi-ethnic Kosovo but that the Albanians had to abide by Serb laws and that I did not wish to discuss greater autonomy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Mr. Robinson, it would be pointless for me to quote from the transcript now of Knut Vollebaek's testimony because it would take up too much time, but this is the gist of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, was there ever any doubt that Kosovo was part of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was never in dispute. And according to the constitution and the legislation, no representative of Serbia had the right to bring into question the status of Kosovo as part of Serbia. Had you agreed to discuss a Kosovo outside the bounds of Serbia, you would have been subject to sanctions under our criminal legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was not the reason. The reason was that Kosovo is part of Serbia. But when he says I told him that Serbian laws had to be in force in Kosovo, is it logical for the laws of the state called Serbia to apply all over its territory?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, logically. This is the case in every country. There has to be a unified legal order, a single legal order, and nothing can deviate from it. You cannot say that the legal order of a certain state does not apply on a certain part of its territory unless that territory is occupied. As long as there is a single state, there has to be a single legal order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were these Serbian laws or were they the laws of the Republic of Serbia which applied equally to Serbs, Albanians, Hungarians, Muslims Ruthenians, Slovaks, Romanians, and all other ethnic groups; that is, all citizens? Did anyone draw up legislation that was favourable only to the Serbs or did laws apply equally to all citizens living on the territory of the state called the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our laws were never ethnically based. They were always state laws applying to all citizens, and all citizens had to comply with them. The state protected the interests of all citizens equally regardless of their ethnic or religious affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the state also protect the ethnic identity of members of ethnic minorities through legislation guaranteeing the use of their languages, education in their own languages, the ability to communicate with government authorities in their own language, including being tried in their mother tongue before the courts?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right to be tried in the mother tongue of the accused was an absolute right that nobody could bring into question. The state not only protected such right for ethnic minorities but also financially supported their implementation. Every year in the budget of Serbia certain funds were set aside to assist media in the languages of ethnic minorities, their newspapers, radio and television stations, and so on and so forth. Many ethnic minorities did not have the funds to finance all this, and they were aided by the state. If the funds provided by the state did not always meet their demands, that's because the state itself was short of funds, but the principle was never encroached upon. Before the aggression against Yugoslavia, there were about 40 newspapers and magazines published in Kosovo in the Albanian language. After our government was formed, as far as I can remember we never banned a single publication. And there was full freedom for the editorial policy of all of these publications. We never interfered with respect to their political standpoints. All that mattered was that they should not perpetrate violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Ratomir Tanic stated here that the Serb authorities attempted to prolong the conflict with the NATO pact in order to increase civilian victims and declare a moral victory. What do you say to this statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It makes no sense. I have facts at my disposal to destroy Ratomir Tanic's credibility. He used to be a collaborator of the state security service of Serbia. He spied on his friends and colleagues for our secret police. After this, he became an agent of foreign intelligence agency and he never denied this. Therefore, any statement made by Ratomir Tanic is questionable because he was an agent of the secret services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's true that they are in dispute, but I wish you to comment on another statement made by him. He said here that we knew that the building of Radio-Television Serbia would be bombed but that we intentionally did not evacuate the employees.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an absolute fabrication. We as the government did not know that the state television building would be bombed. In the night when it was bombed, one of the journalists of the state television was Angelina Vucic, the mother of the Minister of Information, Aleksandar Vucic, a high-ranking functionary of the Serb Radical Party. Had we known that the building would be bombed, the minister would have told his mother to flee and to get out of the way on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Fred Abrahams stated here that the Human Rights Watch report of 1993 describes Kosovo as a police state where the Serb authorities are attempted to move Albanians out of Serb-populated settlements. What do you say about this and can you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. There is no evidence to show that the Serb authorities tried to move out any Albanian settlement, especially not in 1993. There is not a shred of evidence. Of course, Serbia had significant police forces in Kosovo, but their purpose was to preserve public law and order. The Albanians had far greater liberties on Kosovo than existed in other parts of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Many of them did not pay for their utilities, they did not pay taxes, they did not pay their rent, and the authorities never even tried to enforce these claims in order to avoid unpleasant situations. The Albanians, as an ethnic minority, did many things that were illegal, and this was tolerated, and it would not have been tolerated in any other part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't have been tolerated had the person in question been a Serb?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, during the cross-examination of General Obrad Stevanovic, dealing with the same topic that Abrahams dealt with in his testimony, Mr. Nice claimed that all of Serbia was a police state in which the population lived in fear. For example, on page 40115, I quote

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "I return, as we look at things chronologically, to the proposition that [In English] this was indeed a police state and the police state becoming even more extreme as the '90s passed. ... Do you accept from your knowledge of the world generally and from the knowledge of the state in which you operated that where the police or any other otherwise authorised user of force acts with impunity two things follow: The population lives in fear." [Interpretation] Is what Mr. Nice said true, that Serbia was a police state and that the people lived in fear?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By definition, a police state is a state with no legal order in which the self-will of the police rules. Serbia was never in such a situation in all of its history. Of course this doesn't mean that our democracy was perfect. There were certain defects in that respect, but from 1990 to 2000, we had many more civil rights and liberties than after 2000, and we kept increasing these civil rights and liberties. In 1990, we had a situation where the police could arrest a suspect and hold them in custody for three days. After a few years, this was changed and the police could hold an arrested citizen for only one day before handing him over to the investigating judge. When citizens were arrested, a citizen could be detained for a maximum of six months. This has now been extended to two years. I mean, before an indictment is raised. So all kinds of changes have been made. And we used to have the highest international standard ever achieved in that respect. Furthermore, in Serbia, political opponents were very rarely arrested, and I can testify to that because I was practically the only one ever arrested. Mr. Milosevic, you never arrested anyone from those pro-Western parties except Draskovic once or twice when he was causing mayhem on the street, and then you pardoned him, and yet you held me in prison until the last day. To be sure, I never begged you to release me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of this experience of yours, Mr. Seselj, during the 1990s you dealt with the -- you had business with the police, and does your experience show that it was a police state?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the procedural rights were strictly respected. Perhaps a false witness could be brought to bring false accusations against me at a trial, but as for procedural rights, none of these were ever violated in my case, as would have happened in a police state. Where no procedural rights are violated, one cannot speak of a police state. A police state is a state with police self-will ruling, and in our case the police was always subordinate to the authorities. And as I said, we used to have far fewer policemen than are there now in Serbia. We used to have 25.000, and many of these were in Kosovo and Metohija. Now without Kosovo and Metohija, there are 30.000 policemen in Serbia with special powers which they didn't have before to arrest and bring people in. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long were you in prison, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in prison more than once, Mr. Robinson, as I told you when describing my CV. I was convicted to many years in prison. In Belgrade I was arrested seven or eight times and spent brief periods in prison. The first time I was arrested was while I was attending Milovan Djilas's lecture at the Free University in 1984 and I was held for three days. During the time Mr. Milosevic was in power --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And in all cases when you were arrested and subsequently tried and imprisoned, you say that your rights were respected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Procedural rights were respected. It happened once that two false witnesses from rival political parties were brought to say that I had assaulted the speaker of the Assembly physically, and I had not assaulted him physically but only verbally, and I was sentenced to a month. On one occasion one of our deputies threw water on the speaker of the National Assembly and the majority in the Assembly decided that he be taken out. The police came to take him out and we protected him bodily, and I was then sentenced to two months in prison. And the person who threw the water wasn't convicted at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, that was your experience, but I suspect the Prosecution is relying on a wider range of evidence, looking perhaps at the experience of minorities, Kosovo Albanians. Are you in a position to say whether their rights were respected? Is it reasonable to jump from your personal experience to a general conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Until Milosevic came to power, Mr. Milosevic, in the 1980s there were arrests of Albanians for verbal crimes, as happened to people of every ethnic affiliation. After Mr. Milosevic came to power, I guarantee that no Albanian was ever arrested for a verbal offence. They were arrested only for violence or terrorism. And my case is unique in Serbia. As I said, there is no other leader of the opposition who had a fate like mine. And I have to admit, Mr. Robinson, that through frequent provocations on my party -- on my part, I practically forced Mr. Milosevic to take such measures. Sometimes I provoked an incident in order to be arrested because then the strength of my party grew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us proceed with this topic about the police and about the state. During the cross-examination of the same witness, Obrad Stevanovic, General Stevanovic, who testified recently, Mr. Nice said that killings of important persons were not unusual, were not an unusual thing in Serbia. Or, rather, he says: [In English] "I mean in this sense, to be specific: That over the years between 1997 and 2000, in particular, assassination of significant people was a not uncommon event." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there were assassination attempts against -- against members of the regime, Bosko Perosevic, a high official of your party.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to speak one at one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was Bosko Perosevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's stop a minute. If you look at the transcript, you will see that the interpreters are asking you to speak one at a time. You speak the same language, so there is the tendency to -- not to observe the pause between question and answer. Please observe the pause between question and answer. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice gave as examples of such killings the killing of Radovan Stojicevic Badza; Slavko Curuvija; Kelmendi, the lawyer; Fehmi Agani; Arkan; Pavle Bulatovic; Ivan Stambolic. I think that he also mentioned the murder of Zoran Djindjic. Are you aware of any other cases?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a lot of knowledge about these murders. As for Fehmi Agani, he was killed during an incident while the war was still on. I'm not aware of exact circumstances. But it was said that he was killed during an incident as he was trying to leave Serbia. I don't know the exact circumstances. As for the other killings, I personally dealt with this a great deal. You know that I was president of a committee of the federal parliament that was trying to resolve the case of the killing of the Minister of the Interior, Pavle Bulatovic. Our committee came to the possible name of a killer and the possible motives, and then the propaganda machinery of the then government of Zoran Djindjic opened fire at me, saying that I was disclosing secrets, et cetera. And Ivan Delic, who we proved had killed Pavle Bulatovic, was never even questioned. He is well known for different criminal activities of that nature. As for the murder of Radovan Stojicic Badza, he was a colonel general of the police and assistant minister of the interior of Serbia. I learned when hearing Radomir Markovic, also a general, head of the state security service who was then in prison, that Radovan Stojicic Badza was killed because of some links with tobacco smuggling. I directly suspected the well-known Stanko Subotic, Stane Zabac, the frog, who is the king of this Mafia in the Balkans. And the then president, now Prime Minister of Montenegro, Mile Djukanovic, was involved as well. As for the murder of Ivan Stambolic, it has not been resolved yet. Ivan Stambolic was killed a month before the elections of 2000, and the opposition pro-Western parties immediately started accusing you, but at that time Ivan Stambolic was not a political factor at all. No one from government could have had any interest in his murder. Awhile after the killing of Ivan Stambolic, when there had already been a change of government in Serbia, the new government, led by Zoran Djindjic, systematically tried to hush up this murder. It was only when Zoran Djindjic was murdered the authorities stated that they had found the place where the bodily remains of Ivan Stambolic had been buried and they had allegedly found his killers. However, it seemed that the alleged killers were the people who in the putsch of the 5th of October actually brought Djindjic to power. Obviously, Djindjic was killed by the same people who brought him to power because he tried to turn against them at one point. I was also a suspect in terms of Djindjic's assassination. There was an indictment issued against me. A special prosecutor came here to hear me in Belgrade. A year later, the indictment was withdrawn. A minister -- the minister of the interior from Djindjic's government, Dusan Mihajlovic, for a year kept saying that I was behind Djindjic's murder, and now when he published his book of memories in two volumes, he says that I was not involved in any way in Djindjic's killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about these other killings; Kelmendi, Slavko Curuvija, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deal with the Kelmendi killing in great detail. There's nothing special I'd have to say except that I heard that this was an inter-Albanian settling of accounts but I don't know anything else. As for Slavko Curuvija, I publicly called upon the organisers and killers. The regime of Zoran Djindjic did not react to that at all, and in the meantime, those that I had publicly accused of having committed the killing were subsequently killed. As for Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan, he was killed in the beginning of the year 2000, and it is well known who killed him and how. The motive was to take over control over the Belgrade underground so that everything would be ready for the next take-over of government in Serbia. Since it was well known that Zeljko Raznjatovic Arkan was indicted by The Hague Tribunal, he had to stay in Serbia. He could not leave, and due to The Hague Tribunal indictment. So he had to stay in Serbia, thus in charge of the underground. Those who liquidated Arkan took over the underground and instrumentalised the underground in the coup d'etat of the 5th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreters - look at the transcript - they're asking you to slow down, both of you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I didn't hear them. They probably said it on your channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In what capacity did you deal with the investigation of the murder of Pavle Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a federal MP at the initiative of the Serbian Radical Party. Committees were set up of the two chambers of the federal parliament to solve the case of the killing of Pavle Bulatovic, since the Federal Assembly was dissatisfied with the police investigation involved. This committee included representatives of all political parties in parliament, both from Serbia and from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me who it was that you heard. When I say "you," I'm not referring to you only but also other members of the committees.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was primarily in charge of the hearing. We heard many ministers, army and police generals, and other state officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were in charge of these hearings?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I assume that you did not do this on your own. I assume that you were there with a few other members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All members of the committee participated and put questions, but my questions were the most intensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you heard the former head of state security, Radomir Markovic.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By then he was already in the central prison. We sent a request to the president of the district court where he was held in prison, we went to the district prison, and we heard him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about any kind of torture that he had been subjected to?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the reasons why he had been subjected to it?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told us about this, and this was included in the stenographic notes of this committee, that he was illegally taken out of the central prison. According to our legal system, a suspect or an accused person can be taken out of prison only upon instructions from the court in charge. The police absolutely has nothing to do with such a person any longer. They cannot get in contact with him, they cannot hear him; nothing. After being handed over to the investigating judge, he is solely under court jurisdiction. However, the police came to pick him up. He was taken by car to the security institute in Belgrade. That is where Dusan Mihajlovic was, some other high police officials. They organised a luncheon for him, and during this luncheon they were persuading him to testify falsely against you and accuse you of the killing of Ivan Draskovic, the attempted murder of Vuk Draskovic, et cetera, and that, in return, his indictment would be abolished, that they would no longer press charges, that they would give him a false identity, that they would give him plenty of money so that he and his family can live care free in any country of the world, in a country of his choice. I think you have that. I published all the stenographic notes of these hearings, and I think that you therefore have the stenographic notes of the hearing of Radomir Markovic and everything he stated to the members of my committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These stenographic notes published from his hearing is here in tab 12. Could you please find it. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The translation is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will not insist that we read large portions of this transcript. Please open page 156.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Around the middle of the page, it says: "Professor Dr. Vojislav Seselj, while you've been in prison, has somebody been blackmailing you?"

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an old story. I know that from my private information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you know the protocol. We have to find it in our English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Halfway down what is page 2 at the bottom, with the markings 156-160 at the top. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue now, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radomir Markovic is answering: "Mr. Seselj, I was arrested in order to accuse Slobodan Milosevic of being the modus vivendi of all evil and acts of terrorism. "Seselj: Were you taken outside the prison without an order from an investigating judge? "Markovic: Yes, I was. "Seselj: How many times? "Markovic: Once. This comrade took me outside. (Indicates the policeman present.) "Seselj: Who took you outside? "Markovic: Zoran Mijatovic. "Seselj: Where did he take you?" And Zoran Mijatovic was the main chief of the Serbian police at the time. "Seselj: Where did he take you? "Markovic: To a villa of the State Security Service inside the compound of the Security Institute. There is an isolated building there called the villa. He took me there and later, Goran Petrovic and Minister Mihajlovic came. "Seselj: What did they want from you? "Markovic: They wanted me to accuse Slobodan Milosevic, to confess to all those crimes, all those murders, and to say that Slobodan Milosevic directly ordered me to do it. "Seselj: What did they offer you? "Markovic: They offered me a new identity, freedom, money for me and my family in any country I wanted to go to. "Seselj: When you told them that you were not involved in the murders, how did they react? "Markovic: From the very first day, I had told my colleagues who came here to talk to me; I pointed out fundamental shortcomings in the procedure and the statements and testimony taken from the person accusing me. I was hoping that they wanted to help me. I was hoping that they had overlooked something accidentally. I did not know that it was a scenario to accuse me, to place me in such a hopeless position so that I would accuse Milosevic, so that he could be tried and that everything that was done could be justified, that he was the terrorist. You know very well that when they wanted --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we can endure. Ask a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During his hearing, that's what Markovic said to you at an official session of the parliamentary inquiry committee. Was the entire committee there?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not. But at the beginning you have the list of members who were there. In addition to me, Mileta Bulatovic, from the Socialist People's Party of Montenegro; Miodrag Djidic from the Democratic Party, Djindjic's Democratic Party, that is. Veljko Odaljevic from your Socialist Party; and Zelimir Nikcevic from the People's Party of Montenegro. Then there was the official secretary, Godana Perisic [phoen], from the staff of the federal parliament; Milena Vasiljevic, the official stenographer; and Zora Zlatkovic, another official stenographer. The Federal Assembly still has a recording of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was an all-out attack against you because you published these stenographic notes.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
