utterances.text: When we started working, you see, first of all, everybody from the governing regime structures underestimated our possibility of finding anything out through this parliamentary inquiry, and that is how this happened that this parliamentary inquiry was set up. However, we worked very thoroughly. I published a book of 1.000 pages, very small print, including all the stenographic notes and everything else that the committee did. We agreed at the very outset that we be very discreet about everything we find out until we finish our work. When we finished this parliamentary inquiry, when we were to present a report to the Federal Assembly, we agreed that we make the entire material of the parliamentary committee public. As soon as the report was handed in, I gave a large number of journalists large chunks of the transcript, copies of that, and many newspapers started publishing that. That seriously threatened the government in Serbia, the regime of Serbia at the time. Zoran Djindjic was livid. He wanted to press criminal charges against me. This criminal report was actually never put in place but I was informed it was there for years and that it was withdrawn only a few -- only very recently. So the government, the regime was furious because we not only solved the murder of Pavle Bulatovic but realised who committed many other murders. The murder of Pavle Bulatovic and many others show that there were foreign instigators as well, because everybody in Serbia and Montenegro realises that had Pavle Bulatovic lived, Predrag Bulatovic never would have managed to take away Momir Bulatovic's party. This is a sheer coincidence that they all happen to have the same surname, that they come from the same wider family in Montenegro but they're not related. After that, the Americans told Predrag Bulatovic to steal away Momir Bulatovic's party. Had Pavle Bulatovic lived, that would have been impossible in view of his authority and reputation in Montenegro and Serbia and Montenegro. So Pavle Bulatovic's murder had to do with the preparations of the putsch in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the killing of Curuvija? Who did you blame for that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A certain Jorga, then a certain Canda. These are nicknames of well-known criminals in Belgrade. I think Jorga's last name was Jevtovic. I cannot remember now all those names, but it's all there in the book. Curuvija was killed when he was no problem for the regime any longer. He was the owner of Dnevni Telegraf, the dirtiest newspaper ever published in Serbia. We passed a law that was a bit restrictive, a law on the press, and then he had to undergo certain sanctions. They had to close down his newspaper. He stopped publishing his newspaper because he could not pay all the fines that he had to pay because of all the libel suits because of all the lies he published in his newspaper. All of a sudden, when the bombing had already started, he got killed. Of course, for a long time this murder was hushed up. There were rumours that the state security service was involved based on reports about them keeping him under surveillance, but nobody from the current authorities actually solved that murder. The man was also involved in some financial scandals, smuggling contraband, but probably this is of no interest to the Court here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you see how you just spoke? The last sentence. That was modulated. Try to maintain that tone, because it's becoming very, very difficult for me to concentrate. You just achieved a tone, a level that is perfectly acceptable. See whether you can maintain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, maybe that is the consequence of fear that you instilled in me by saying that you would put an end to my testimony if I failed to rise again when you enter. Maybe the fear is still having a hold on me and suppressing my adrenaline. But please do not expect me to speak as Mr. Nice speaks. My wife would leave me immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The decibel level was just as high before. But you just achieved a very moderate tone and let us try and maintain that. I think it's in the interest of everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try, but I'm tired now, and maybe the decibel level is the result of that. However, if I raise my voice again, please know that it's not deliberate and it's not intended to interfere with your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In fact, I have distinctly said it's not deliberate and not meant to be offensive. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me come back to my question, Mr. Seselj; namely, something that Mr. Nice said when cross-examining General Obrad Stevanovic. The years between 1997 and 2000, in particular the assassination of several people, assassinations of people were not an uncommon event. Let us not limit ourselves to this period 1997 to 2000 that Mr. Nice mentioned. Let us take it from 1989 to 2000. Was there a single opposition leader who was killed in that period?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not a single opposition leader was killed. It was only criminals who were killed, usually in mutual settlements of account in the underground. But high officials of the regime were sometimes killed as well, people who enjoyed your trust. Radovan Stojicic Badza was a man of your inner circle who was completely loyal to you. I know that for a fact, although this man Badza arrested me on one occasion in Gnjilane, put me in prison for two months, but I have to tell the truth here and testify about facts. There were two attempts to assassinate Vuk Draskovic. That much is true. That is the only opposition leader who is the subject of assassination attempts. However, the circumstances were always very strange. The first was on the Ibarska highway when a truck full of sand suddenly sprang in front of him and his driver and his wife's brother were killed on the spot. Draskovic was unscathed. That looked very strange to me, although our police, traffic police, said immediately it was simply a traffic accident. I, however, found the circumstances bizarre. The investigation started, and then it emerged that the truck belonged to the state security service. The state security officers were involved, et cetera, et cetera. The subject was very unpleasant to the authorities, and it later turned out that the same people who were suspected of trying to assassinate Vuk Draskovic were those who placed Zoran Djindjic in power. Zoran Djindjic was -- in fact, Vuk Draskovic was always on the ready to take over power if a clash happened between you and me. You always kept Draskovic in the hope that he would form a coalition government with you. And then comes this assassination attempt on Draskovic. Who was the most bothered by Draskovic at the time? I can say with full responsibility that Djindjic found him most bothersome. Several months later, there was another assassination attempt on Vuk Draskovic in Budva. Very strange. The assassin fired two bullets, each one failing to graze him, to graze his ears, and he remained uninjured. Draskovic was in Budva where he had an apartment and the police of Montenegro always provided him with security to stand in front of his apartment. On the day of that assassination attempt, the police in Montenegro failed to provide the security detail. They obviously knew what was in the offing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have given a full answer. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on then. I didn't ask for this in particular, but I suppose, Mr. Robinson, that the exhibits that have already been quoted and have been presented in good order with translations can be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The following tabs are admitted: 1, 2, 3, 12, 25 in relation to chapter 19, 30, and 31. There is also Ivan Kristan's article in Socialism. Do you want that last one?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What's the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D303, tab 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it hadn't been previously exhibited, no translation at present, therefore it will presumably be on your usual terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. No translation, so it's marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. I understand that it is only the article of Mr. Kristan from the Socialism magazine is without the translation. The other documents all have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All have -- I see, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, witness Fehim Elshani, who testified here in February Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 2002, transcript page 838, stated the following: "During the war in Kosovo, Serb forces issued a communique saying that in the case of an attack by NATO, they would retaliate against Albanian population." This was stated not by Serb forces but the Serb government through its leaders in public communiques. You were a deputy Prime Minister. Is this true, what this witness says?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true. The entire public in our country followed carefully all the communiques of the government and we see that this is a flagrant lie. There was no such communique ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness Mahmut Bakalli enumerated some people who were not prepared to negotiate. Among others, he named Tomislav Nikolic, deputy president of Seselj's Radical Party. Is that true? He testified on the 18th of February, 2002, and that's on transcript page 538. So he's talking about your deputy, Tomislav Nikolic. Was he among the people who were not prepared to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This again is absolutely untrue. Tomislav Nikolic was a member of the delegation of Serbia and he travelled to Kosovo many times, to Pristina, for negotiations with Albanian political parties. Unfortunately, without any success. But you can judge for yourself about the veracity of Mahmut Bakalli when you know that Mahmut Bakalli called Zoran Djindjic the most dangerous Serb nationalist just several days before Djindjic was murdered. All Serbian newspapers published this several days before Zoran Djindjic's death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Another witness, Agim Berisha, said that Seselj had stated that he would expel all Albanians to the other side of the Prokletije mountains. That is transcript page 965, and he testified on the 20th of February, 2002.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is absolutely untrue. You have already seen a passage from my speech where I said that Albanian immigrants who do not have Serbian citizenship and at the same time hold separatist views would have to be expelled. Any country would do the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was more specific. He said you would expel them to the other side of Prokletije mountains.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that may have been a figure of speech because Prokletije mountains are the highest in the area. That would have involved a bit of mountaineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He said on the same day, on page 967, that he had heard from Seselj of a special plan that was in existence, and he says, "We were afraid for our lives because we were only civilians locked up in our homes." And when I asked him on that 26th of February where exactly Seselj stated he would expel Albanians across Prokletije mountains, he answered he didn't know whether he read about it in the newspapers or heard about it on television, and he wasn't sure whether Seselj was speaking about Albanians as such or about the KLA. Could you comment.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously those people who coached this witness in his false testimony didn't do a good job, so he got confused in the witness box. He didn't know what to say. The only obvious thing is that he was lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now we have something rather special. Witness Konaj, who testified on the 25th of April, 2002, transcript page 3788. He says that police vehicles escorted Seselj's convoy, that one of these vehicles came into the intersection between Gorazdevac and Loxhe, and there they came across some children playing ball, and then they abused those children, killing Tahir Halaj -- or Shalaj, on the day.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that when I visited certain crisis areas in Kosovo in the summer of 1998, I visited Gorazdevac, which is not far from Pec. There was a police escort, but during my entire stay in Kosovo and Metohija there was not a single incident. The rest is the witness's fabrication. Whether something like that happened in some other place far away from where I was, whether somebody was indeed killed, I don't know. Maybe. But not a single incident was linked to my visit to Kosovo. I was never even insulted verbally once, nor did my escort threaten anybody. But it's true that I had a police escort; one car in front us and one car behind us. I also had journalists with me, as I usually did during all my visits and tours, because that was one of the purposes, to spread the word that I was looking for a political solution, for negotiations, et cetera. And I also visited Serb settlements to persuade people not to move to Serbia, because at one point the population of Gorazde, which is a purely Serb place, said that they were going to move to Serbia because they couldn't stand it any longer. They couldn't stand the pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A protected witness, K5, stated on the 27th of May, 2002, transcript page 5549, that there existed paramilitary groups in Kosovo that belonged to Seselj, as he says, and that were called White Eagles. Is this correct, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I never had any kind of paramilitary groups. Second, I never had anything to do with any White Eagles. And for the entire duration of the war in Kosovo and Metohija, and even before, during fighting with terrorist groups in Kosovo and Metohija, there were no Serb paramilitary units from Serbia at any point. The government had a very clear policy in that respect; namely, that we had to prevent the emergence of any paramilitary units. There had been bad experience from previous wars in Bosnia and in Croatia, and we wanted to avoid the repetition of such experience at all cost. There were no paramilitary groups in Kosovo whatsoever. There was only the army of Yugoslavia and the police of Serbia who were active in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea why this expression, why this term "White Eagles" is used? Was this term ever used in relation to your party or the volunteers from your party? Is there any link whatsoever between the term "White Eagles" and your party?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In previous wars there was a small paramilitary organisation called White Eagles, but the Serb Radical Party had absolutely nothing to do with them. On the contrary, we always kept our distance from them and similar organisations, believing that they are doing a great damage to the Serb people because their main motivation was looting and self-interest. However, they never even appeared in Kosovo. And there were even claims in Western media that Arkan was in Kosovo with his volunteers guard. But Arkan spent the entire war in Kosovo in the Hyatt Hotel in Belgrade, and he was in the plain view of all the foreign press that were staying in the same hotel, despite the fact that we were practically bombarded by these claims in the Western media about Arkan's presence in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Shukri Buja, when asked whether he was surprised by the police attack on Racak, answered in the negative. He explained that there had been warnings about the arrival of Seselj and the activities of the so-called Red Hand or Red Arm -- Black Arm, sorry.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is pure fabrication. There was an organisation called Black Hand about 100 years ago. It was a creation of the Obrenovic royal family, who staged a coup, and in 1903 [Realtime transcript read in error "'93"] they were replaced by the Karadjordjevic family, and this organisation was supposed to threaten to kill Aleksandar Karadjordjevic. But this is completely made up as far as the recent wars are concerned. There was no such organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript has a figure '93. Did you say 1903?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1903. In 1903 there was a change of dynasty in Serbia through a military coup d'etat. A group of military officers organised themselves into an organisation called the Black Hand, and there was a change in the ruling royal family. As I said, this happened over a hundred years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness Shukri Buja stated, and that's on page 6421 of the transcript on the 6th of June, 2002, that video clips of Radio-Television Serbia can be found showing Seselj in a military uniform reviewing his units, as was the case with Arkan. Is this correct? Please be precise. Tell us first of all, did you have any units of your own; and secondly, did you ever review or inspect your units?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV SESELJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I never have any of -- units of my own. During the war in Serbian Krajina and the beginning of the civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Serb Radical Party had its volunteers but exclusively as part of the JNA, which was the only legal military force on the territory of the former Yugoslavia. In Kosovo and Metohija, we never had any volunteers from the Serb Radical Party. The members of our party who were military conscripts were mobilised into military units, and one of our deputies was even killed. He was a captain first class and a reservist of the Yugoslav army in the war on Kosovo and Metohija. However, we never called for volunteers. If there were volunteers in Kosovo and Metohija, they apply directly to the units of the army of Yugoslavia on their own initiative. I wore a uniform for a period when touring military positions in Serbian Krajina at the time when the SFRY existed, when every citizen could be considered a member of the armed forces if he was fighting the enemy in an organised manner with weapons in his hands. As soon as Yugoslavia dissolved, when first Slovenia and then Croatia and then Bosnia and Herzegovina were internationally recognised, I stopped wearing a uniform when visiting Serb forces in various theatres of war, which I visited frequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we will adjourn for the day and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.
